Proposed compensation would be case observation fees only, subject to the usual fair-market-value review, compliance documentation, and confirmation of actual educational need. Neither physician should be positioned as a speaker or consultant until the initial observation activity is complete and feedback is reviewed.

4. Messaging and next steps
Anika asked whether agency materials need revision before the next KOL cycle. Carlos said the immediate priority is preparation for Feld’s registry-data questions and alignment with Clinical. The group agreed to convene a short call with Dr. Leon Adeyemi to develop appropriate talking points and identify any materials that should not be used until further review.

Action Items

| Schedule call with Dr. Adeyemi regarding talking points for Dr. Feld’s registry questions | Carlos Mendes | July 16, 2021 |

Design History File — Engineering Memorandum

Date: 2 April 2019
From: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
Subject: Design Change Rationale — ECO-2019-118 (Cup Rim Geometry)
Distribution: DHF file copy; cc Priya Raman, Carlos Mendes

1. Purpose

This memo documents the technical basis for proposed engineering change order ECO-2019-118, which would modify the acetabular cup rim geometry on ApexHip to reduce edge-loading wear observed at higher cup inclination angles. It also records the current disposition of the change.

2. Background

Per DR-3 (Nov 2016), the wear-test protocol adopted for ApexHip design verification used ISO 14242 methodology at a fixed 45° cup inclination angle only. That was consistent with prevailing industry practice for MoM bearings at the time and was reviewed and approved by the design review board. No testing was performed at higher inclination angles during original verification.

In Feb 2019 I re-ran wear testing (Meridian Testing Labs, report attached as Apex_wear_55deg_rev2.xlsx) at 55° inclination to evaluate performance under conditions more representative of real-world cup positioning variability, prompted by field data patterns I'd been informally tracking. Results showed volumetric wear rates 4-6x higher than the 45° baseline, consistent with an edge-loading mechanism at the cup rim under elevated inclination. This is a materially different wear regime than what our original verification testing characterized.

I flagged these results to Priya Raman and Carlos Mendes in Feb 2019 (see my 2/14/19 memo). This ECO is the engineering follow-up.

3. Proposed Change

ECO-2019-118 would modify the cup rim profile (increased rim coverage/reduced chamfer angle) to reduce the incidence and severity of edge loading at inclination angles above the 45° baseline, without materially changing head diameter compatibility or the KinetiCoat ingrowth surface.

4. Alternatives Considered

a. Full redesign of rim geometry per above — addresses root mechanism directly but requires new tooling and re-verification.
b. No hardware change; instead issue supplemental surgical technique guidance to surgeons emphasizing target cup inclination angle (recommend tightening guidance toward 40-45° with instrumentation aids) to reduce the incidence of high-inclination placements in the field.
c. No action — not recommended; field inclination variability is well documented in the literature and cannot be assumed to trend toward the 45° baseline on its own.

5. Cost and Timeline (Option a)

Tooling changes for the modified rim profile are estimated at $2.1M, primarily new injection/machining tooling at Cork plus revalidation. Estimated timeline to implementation is approximately 9 months, including design verification testing at both 45° and 55° inclination, updated FMEA, and a supplemental 510(k) or letter-to-file determination pending regulatory review.

6. Recommendation

I recommend pursuing either (a) the rim redesign or, at minimum, (b) updated surgical technique guidance as an interim mitigation while a redesign is evaluated. Given the magnitude of the wear multiplier at 55°, I don't think no-action is defensible from an engineering standpoint, though I recognize the clinical significance of this lab-scale finding relative to actual field revision rates is still an open question.

7. Disposition

This change has been discussed with Quality and Product Management. Per direction from management, ECO-2019-118 is deferred at this time pending additional clinical correlation data (i.e., whether registry/complaint trends support a wear-driven revision signal sufficient to justify the tooling investment and field guidance change). This memo and the underlying test data are retained in the DHF for future reference should the ECO be reopened.

Tom Halvorsen
Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip

ENGINEERING TEST SUMMARY REPORT

Date: 18 April 2019
Prepared by: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer
Product: KneeFlex Total Knee System
Subject: Meridian Testing Labs KneeFlex Wear Report Summary

Purpose

This report summarizes the final results from Meridian Testing Labs’ simulator wear evaluation of the KneeFlex tibial insert. Testing was run to the ISO 14243 knee wear simulation protocol through five million cycles. This is the production-intent UHMWPE tibial insert paired with the standard KneeFlex cobalt-chromium femoral component.

Bottom line: wear performance is where we expected it to be. No station showed an outlier trend that would require a design or material investigation.

Test Configuration

Meridian tested six stations using 10 mm medium congruent KneeFlex tibial inserts. The inserts were gamma-sterilized, packaged production-equivalent parts from the 2018 pilot build. Femoral components were standard polished Co/Cr components. Testing used bovine serum lubricant at the concentration specified in the protocol, with periodic lubricant changes and soak controls for fluid uptake correction.

The loading and motion profile followed ISO 14243 conditions. Inspections and gravimetric measurements were completed at one million cycle intervals. Meridian also performed visual inspection of the articular surfaces at each pull point.

Results

Corrected wear volume at five million cycles is summarized below.

| Test Station | Tibial Insert Size | Wear Volume at 5M Cycles (mm³) | Average Wear Rate (mm³/MC) | Observations |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| 1 | 10 mm Medium | 37.8 | 7.6 | Uniform polish, no delamination |
| 2 | 10 mm Medium | 41.2 | 8.2 | Minor medial polish |
| 3 | 10 mm Medium | 39.6 | 7.9 | No unusual surface findings |
| 4 | 10 mm Medium | 43.1 | 8.6 | Light anterior contact polish |
| 5 | 10 mm Medium | 38.9 | 7.8 | No unusual surface findings |
| 6 | 10 mm Medium | 40.5 | 8.1 | Uniform polish, no delamination |

Mean corrected wear volume was 40.2 mm³ at five million cycles, with a station-to-station range of 37.8 to 43.1 mm³. Mean calculated wear rate was 8.0 mm³ per million cycles.

The control specimens showed the expected fluid uptake behavior. Meridian applied the soak-control correction before reporting the final values above. Raw mass-loss data and the control data are retained in Meridian report MTL-KF-19-044 and the accompanying electronic worksheet.

Surface Findings

Visual review did not identify cracking, pitting, delamination, or gross material loss on any test insert. The expected polished contact regions were present on the medial and lateral bearing surfaces. Station 4 had slightly more visible anterior polish than the other stations, but its gravimetric result remained within the overall range and there was no associated damage pattern.

There were no mechanical interruptions, fixture failures, or protocol deviations reported by Meridian during the five-million-cycle run.

Conclusion

The KneeFlex tibial insert demonstrated acceptable wear performance under the tested ISO 14243 simulator conditions through five million cycles. Results are consistent across all six stations and support continued use of the current insert geometry and material specification.

Meridian’s final signed report, MTL-KF-19-044, and the station-level measurement workbook have been placed in the KneeFlex design verification folder. No additional simulator testing is recommended from these results alone.

Subject: NJR 2021 annual report - ApexHip 5-year revision rate

Priya, Dana, Tom,

The UK National Joint Registry (NJR) 2021 annual data tables were released this morning. I pulled our extract and ran the survival curves for the primary total hip cohort.

The headline number is problematic: the ApexHip 5-year cumulative revision rate is currently sitting at 7.1% (95% CI: 6.2% – 8.1%). For comparison, the contemporary class average across uncemented metal-on-poly and ceramic constructs in the registry is tracking at 3.2% at the 5-year mark. Even when adjusting for age stratification and diagnosis (predominantly osteoarthritis in the active 45–65 subset), Apex is more than double the benchmark.

Most concerning is the revision diagnosis breakdown. A significant portion of the early failures in the registry cohort cite aseptic loosening, adverse soft tissue reaction, or pain secondary to metallosis. This directly mirrors the trajectory we have been observing internally in TrackWise with the metal-ion complaint trend dating back to the Atlanta cluster in August 2018 (e.g., TW-2018-0882 et seq.) and the subsequent adverse reaction reports. The registry signal and our internal vigilance data are now pointing to the exact same failure mode.

Given the magnitude of the delta, we cannot treat this as standard PMS monitoring. I strongly recommend escalating this to a formal Registry Signal Review meeting with Leon and Carlos. Depending on how the clinical review lands, we may need to evaluate our continued marketing stance and labeling updates in short order.

Let me know your availability later this week to walk through the Kaplan-Meier plots.

VERIDIAN ORTHOPEDICS, INC.
Internal Communications Briefing — Speaker Notes

Date: February 12, 2024
Prepared by: Anika Shah, Director, Marketing Communications
Subject: Notes for internal comms briefing — messaging retrospective

Slide 1 — Why we are doing this

This is not a product relaunch discussion, and it is not an exercise in assigning blame to an individual or team. We need to be candid about how ApexHip messaging evolved, what we knew when particular materials were approved, and where our process did not keep pace with the information coming in from the field and the registries.

Apex was positioned from launch around active adults, large-head stability, low wear, and longevity. The “Active Life” work gave the product a clear identity, but it also created pressure to keep the story simple and positive after the evidence became more complicated.

Slide 2 — Claims used over time

Key language in brochures, speaker materials, and sales presentations included:

- “Designed for a lifetime of movement.”
- “Large-head stability for active patients.”
- “Low-wear performance engineered for demanding lifestyles.”
- Comparisons suggesting favorable revision performance versus conventional alternatives.
- “Confidence to return to the activities that matter.”

Not every phrase appeared in every piece, and several were appropriately qualified in professional-facing materials. Still, in aggregate, the messaging communicated durability and sustained performance more strongly than the supporting record justified.

Slide 3 — The 2020 revision-comparison slide

The 2020 commercial slide comparing Apex revision experience with class benchmarks was created from data available at that time. It predated the March 2021 NJR annual report, which identified ApexHip’s five-year revision rate at 7.1% compared with a 3.2% class average.

That timing matters. The slide was not built using the March 2021 NJR result. But once that result was available, we should have revisited the slide, its continued circulation, and the broader durability narrative sooner. We did not have an effective trigger requiring Marketing Communications to re-open previously approved claims when registry information materially changed.

Slide 4 — What we should have done differently

We relied too heavily on point-in-time substantiation. Claim review cannot end at approval, particularly for an implanted device with long-term outcomes that develop over years.

Going forward, claims with clinical-performance implications need:

1. A named business owner and clinical owner.
2. A defined review interval.
3. Immediate reassessment following material registry signals, complaint trends, labeling changes, or field safety communications.
4. Clearer documentation of what data support a claim, what data limit it, and when the claim was last reviewed.

Slide 5 — Closing message

The lesson is not that Marketing should interpret clinical data independently. The lesson is that we need a disciplined route for clinical, PMS, Regulatory, and Marketing to revisit messaging together when the evidence changes. We should have asked harder questions earlier, especially about whether our old materials remained appropriate after the NJR signal.

4400 Silver Lake Blvd.

June 14, 2022

FDA CDRH
Office of Compliance

Re: Voluntary Recall Notification - ApexHip Acetabular Cup Lots V-2200 to V-2299
FDA Recall No. Z-1418-2022

To Whom It May Concern:

Veridian Orthopedics, Inc. hereby notifies the Food and Drug Administration of a voluntary Class II recall of specified ApexHip acetabular cup lots. The affected devices are ApexHip cobalt/chromium acetabular cups with KinetiCoat porous titanium coating, manufactured at Veridian’s Cork, Ireland facility.

The recall applies to cup lots V-2200 through V-2299, manufactured from November 2021 through February 2022. A total of 1,140 units were distributed in the United States. Based on the current lot-trace reconciliation, 412 units have been implanted. The balance is located in customer or distributor inventory, has been returned, or remains in Veridian-controlled inventory pending final reconciliation.

The recall was initiated following incoming-inspection reports from two hospital customers, including Northgate Health System and a Denver-area hospital. In each report, flaking of the KinetiCoat coating was observed upon removal of the device from its packaging. No other ApexHip lots are included in this action.

Veridian’s investigation has identified plasma-spray parameter drift following a chamber maintenance event at the Cork facility as the probable root cause of the coating adhesion failures. Review of applicable batch records, chamber data, and maintenance documentation supports this conclusion. The investigation remains open, and Veridian will provide supplemental information should additional findings affect the scope or assessment of this action.

Immediate corrective actions include: (1) cessation of distribution for the affected lots; (2) segregation and inventory reconciliation of affected product; (3) inspection and requalification of the plasma-spray chamber; (4) verification of plasma-spray operating parameters and associated monitoring controls; and (5) review and revision, as appropriate, of maintenance and post-maintenance release procedures. The chamber will not be returned to routine production until requalification requirements have been completed and approved by Quality.

Customer notification letters are being sent concurrently to all known consignees, with instructions to identify, cease use of, and return affected product. Veridian will conduct effectiveness checks and provide periodic status reports in accordance with FDA requirements.

This action concerns a coating adhesion issue and is not related to metal-ion wear or other field performance concerns associated with ApexHip.

Please contact me at (574) 555-0142 or dokonkwo@veridianortho.com with any questions.

Sincerely,

Dana Okonkwo
Vice President, Regulatory Affairs
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.

2. Quality Process Alignment: In light of the June 2021 FDA Form 483 Observation 2 citing complaint trending timeliness, HR strongly recommends Quality initiate an immediate resource allocation and procedural review to prevent further systemic processing bottlenecks.

Apex Revenue Impact Model — Q4 2022 Scenarios
Prepared by: Hannah Berg, FP&A Manager
Date: October 14, 2022
To: Owen Park, CFO
Subject: Apex Revenue Impact Model - Q4 2022 Scenarios

Attached: `Apex_Revenue_Impact_Model_Q4_2022_v5.xlsx`

Owen,

Per our discussion, I refreshed the Apex model using September actuals and the current field forecast. The model is intended to frame revenue exposure through FY24; it does not attempt to estimate claim severity or timing.

Apex FY22 is now expected to close at approximately $71.0M, versus the $96.0M peak in FY20. The decline began before the June cup recall in the underlying order data. The more pronounced step-down follows the September 2021 labeling update and what Sales characterizes as increased surgeon caution after the NJR data circulated. The recall remains a separate, lot-specific assumption in the model, although several field teams report customers are not making that distinction.

Summary output ($M):

| Scenario | FY22E | FY23E | FY24E | FY22–FY24 Change |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Status quo / current label | 71.0 | 62.4 | 60.1 | (15%) |
| Label-driven decline | 71.0 | 54.7 | 45.9 | (35%) |
| Full market withdrawal | 71.0 | 48.3 | 42.6 | (40%) |

The status quo case assumes current labeling remains in place, no broad commercial action, and modest attrition offset by existing account utilization. It is the closest to the current Sales operating plan, though I would not characterize it as the base case with high confidence.

The label-driven decline case assumes continued loss of new implanters, lower utilization among accounts that have moved Apex to a limited-use position, and increasing price concessions where distributors seek to retain volume. This case reflects the present trajectory in the Southeast and selected Midwest accounts more closely than the operating plan.

The withdrawal case assumes no new commercial placements after an orderly market action, with only limited residual revenue from contracted inventory and replacement requirements. This is necessarily a planning construct, not a recommendation regarding product status.

For reserve adequacy testing, I recommend using the full withdrawal scenario as the conservative revenue sensitivity. It produces the lowest contribution available to absorb claims-related costs and avoids relying on a recovery in surgeon confidence that we are not seeing in the current forecast submissions.

I have kept the $18M Q3 reserve as a separate line item in the workbook and have not assumed any insurance recoveries. We can walk through the account-level assumptions Monday if helpful.

Hannah

POST-MARKET SURVEILLANCE & REGISTRY ANALYTICS

MEMORANDUM

TO: Dana Okonkwo (VP Regulatory Affairs), Priya Raman (Director Quality & Complaint Handling), Dr. Leon Adeyemi (Chief Medical Officer)
FROM: Greg Novak (Director, Post-Market Surveillance)
DATE: March 22, 2021
SUBJECT: NJR 2021 Annual Report – ApexHip 5-Year Revision Rate Analysis

Executive Summary

The UK National Joint Registry (NJR) has released its 2021 Annual Report data tables, incorporating cumulative implant survival figures through December 31, 2020.

Our initial data extraction for the ApexHip Total Hip System reveals a statistically significant adverse survival divergence. The cumulative 5-year revision rate for ApexHip is reported at 7.1% (95% CI: 6.2%–8.1%), compared to a class benchmark of 3.2% (95% CI: 3.0%–3.4%) across contemporaneous metal-on-metal (MoM) and hybrid construct cohorts in the registry.

Cohort Breakdown and Timing of Divergence

The NJR dataset captures 4,128 primary ApexHip procedures performed across UK centers since CE mark entry in September 2017:

*   Total Implants Tracked: 4,128 units (primarily 48mm–54mm acetabular cup sizes paired with matching Co/Cr femoral heads).
*   Total Revisions Recorded: 184 cases.
*   Revision Rate Trajectory:
    *   *Year 1:* 1.2% (ApexHip) vs. 0.9% (Class average)
    *   *Year 2:* 2.4% (ApexHip) vs. 1.7% (Class average)
    *   *Year 3:* 4.6% (ApexHip) vs. 2.3% (Class average)
    *   *Year 5:* 7.1% (ApexHip) vs. 3.2% (Class average)

The performance curve begins to diverge distinctly between months 24 and 36. Primary indications cited for revision within the NJR return entries include "pain of unknown origin," "aseptic loosening/cup migration," and "adverse soft tissue reaction" (accounting for roughly 48% of coded revision rationales past the 36-month mark).

Next Steps & Recommendations

1.  AJRR Cross-Validation: We must correlate these findings against domestic performance immediately. American Joint Replacement Registry (AJRR) annual procedural datasets are slated for release later in 2021. I strongly recommend we prepare an identical query syntax to interrogate US revision trajectories as soon as that raw data cuts become available.
2.  Clinical Assessment: I request Dr. Adeyemi’s formal clinical read regarding whether a 7.1% 5-year cumulative revision rate crosses our established Post-Market Clinical Follow-up (PMCF) internal action thresholds, particularly given the elevated proportion of soft-tissue and aseptic indications.
3.  Formal Signal Review: Under our post-market surveillance SOPs, this variance warrants convening an interdepartmental Registry Signal Review meeting among Regulatory Affairs, Quality, Clinical, and Product Engineering to determine if labeling amendments, field communications, or formal CAPA escalation are required.

Please let me know your availability later this week to discuss these initial figures.

TO: Complaint Investigation File (TrackWise)
FROM: Priya Raman, Director, Quality & Complaint Handling
DATE: September 10, 2018
SUBJECT: MDR Reportability Assessment – TW-2018-0311, TW-2018-0322, TW-2018-0340
CC: Dana Okonkwo, VP Regulatory Affairs; Devon Mitchell, Sr. Regulatory Specialist

1. Purpose & Scope
This memorandum documents the Medical Device Reporting (MDR) reportability determination per internal procedure SOP-QA-404 (*Adverse Event Reporting and MDR Decision Trees*) and 21 CFR 803.50 for three recent complaint files originating from Dr. Marcus Feld’s clinical practice (Atlanta Joint Institute). All three cases involve the Veridian ApexHip Acetabular Cup system paired with Co/Cr modular heads.

2. File Assessments

A. TrackWise Record: TW-2018-0322
* Device Identification: ApexHip Cup, 52 mm (Lot V-2041); ApexHip Femoral Head, 40 mm (Lot H-3118). Implanted October 2017.
* Clinical Presentation: Patient presented at 10 months post-op with persistent groin pain, swelling, and reduced range of motion. Serum cobalt levels measured at 11.4 µg/L; chromium at 8.2 µg/L. Aspiration and MARS MRI revealed extensive local fluid collection and soft tissue inflammation consistent with metallosis. Dr. Feld has scheduled a revision surgery for October 4, 2018 to explant the acetabular and femoral bearing components.
* MDR Determination: REPORTABLE. Under 21 CFR 803.50(a)(1), this event constitutes a reportable serious injury. The event necessitated surgical intervention (revision arthroplasty) to preclude permanent impairment of a body structure/function resulting from local tissue reaction and adverse local tissue response (ALTR).

B. TrackWise Record: TW-2018-0340
* Device Identification: ApexHip Cup, 56 mm (Lot V-2044); ApexHip Femoral Head, 44 mm (Lot H-3142). Implanted December 2017.
* Clinical Presentation: Patient reported severe pain and gait instability at 8 months. Whole blood cobalt was confirmed at 14.1 µg/L. Ultrasound-guided aspiration recovered turbid, dark-stained synovial fluid indicative of metal debris. Operative notes from Dr. Feld recommend urgent revision due to progressive tissue necrosis and pseudotumor formation.
* MDR Determination: REPORTABLE. In accordance with 21 CFR 803.50, this case satisfies the criteria for serious injury requiring medical/surgical intervention to prevent irreversible tissue damage.

C. TrackWise Record: TW-2018-0311
* Device Identification: ApexHip Cup, 50 mm (Lot V-2039); ApexHip Femoral Head, 38 mm (Lot H-3094). Implanted September 2017.
* Clinical Presentation: Initial complaint indicated mild trochanteric bursitis and an initial cobalt draw of 6.2 µg/L. Radiographs demonstrate well-fixed components with no observable osteolysis or pseudotumor. Revision has not been recommended; the patient is undergoing physical therapy.
* MDR Determination: NON-REPORTABLE AT THIS TIME (HELD PENDING DATA). The current clinical presentation does not meet the serious injury threshold under 21 CFR 803.3. File is held pending secondary laboratory cobalt retest data and clinical follow-up records from the clinic, expected by September 24, 2018.

3. Action Items
1. Quality has updated the MDR disposition blocks in TrackWise for TW-2018-0322 and TW-2018-0340 to "Reportable."
2. Recommend Devon Mitchell prepare draft initial FDA Form 3500A submissions for lots V-2041 and V-2044 to ensure timely submission within the 30-day statutory clock.
3. Post-Market Surveillance will maintain active monitoring on TW-2018-0311 (Lot V-2039) pending retest panels.

Priya, Dana,

I have finalized the Q3 2018 post-market surveillance complaint trending analysis for the ApexHip system.

The primary signal of note this quarter involves adverse event reports associated with suspected metal-ion release and local tissue reactions. For Q3, metal-ion related complaints increased from our historical baseline of roughly 0.3% of cumulative sales/implants to 0.6% (14 reported events against approximately 2,350 implants distributed during the quarter).

This represents the first quarter exhibiting a statistically noticeable uptick since the April 2017 launch. Looking closely at the data, the increase is driven substantially by the Atlanta cluster logged in TrackWise during August (specifically cases originating out of Dr. Feld’s group, e.g., TW-2018-0882, TW-2018-0884, TW-2018-0891).

While the shift from 0.3% to 0.6% triggers our internal screening threshold for closer scrutiny, the overall complaint rate remains within historical noise bands documented in the literature for contemporary orthopedic MoM devices. At this juncture, our control charts do not indicate a formal out-of-spec process shift under SOP-PMS-04.

I recommend continued tight monitoring without escalating to a formal trending CAPA today, with a dedicated follow-up review scheduled at the close of Q4 to determine if this is an isolated regional outlier or an emerging broader trend.

Let me know if you would like me to pull together additional subgroup stratifications by head diameter or cup size prior to next week’s Quality review.

National Sales Meeting 2018
ApexHip Positioning Deck — Speaker Notes

Presenter: Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip
Date: January 18, 2018
Session: Reconstructive Portfolio Breakout
Distribution: Field Sales and Marketing

Slide 1 — Why Apex, Why Now

Open with the patient, not the bearing. The ApexHip patient is generally an active adult who expects to remain active: working, traveling, cycling, golf, family life. We have an opportunity to offer a modern total hip platform designed around stability, range of motion, and durable materials.

Do not frame ClassicHip as a bad product. It remains an important, proven option and is appropriate for many patients. The positioning is choice: ClassicHip is our established metal-on-poly platform; ApexHip gives the surgeon another option for the active, appropriately selected patient who values a large-head construct and a contemporary fixation platform.

Suggested line: “Apex expands the conversation beyond simply getting back to walking. It is designed for the patient who wants confidence in movement.”

Slide 2 — Differentiating the Platform

The three pillars are:

1. Stability through large-head options. Apex offers head sizes from 36 to 50 mm, allowing surgeons to select a construct that supports stability and range of motion.

2. Wear performance. In our ISO 14242 bench testing at standard 45-degree cup inclination, Apex demonstrated lower early wear rates than legacy systems. Keep this statement tied to the test conditions and use the approved leave-behind if a surgeon asks for data.

3. Fixation. The acetabular cup uses KinetiCoat porous titanium coating, acquired with KBT, to support bone ingrowth and initial fixation.

Avoid getting drawn into a head-to-head “winner” discussion with every competitor. We do not need to name brands to make the point. Most competitive systems can offer a large head or porous coating; Apex brings those features together in a coherent system backed by Veridian’s reconstructive organization.

Slide 3 — KinetiCoat: Make It Concrete

Reps should be comfortable explaining the coating in plain language. KinetiCoat is not paint and should never be described that way. It is a porous titanium coating applied to the cup surface to create a structure intended to support bone ingrowth over time.

Suggested language: “The goal is biologic fixation. KinetiCoat gives the surgeon a porous surface designed to help the patient’s bone engage with the cup.”

Do not overstate this as faster healing, guaranteed fixation, or superior fixation in every patient. Use “designed to support” and “intended to promote” consistently.

Slide 4 — Handling the Longevity Question

This is important: do not promise a specific number of years. We have bench data and a strong engineering rationale, but clinical follow-up for Apex is still short. Do not tell a surgeon or patient that Apex will last 20 years, 25 years, or “a lifetime.”

If asked, say: “Apex was designed with durability in mind, and the available bench testing supports its wear-performance profile. As with any newer system, long-term clinical follow-up continues to accumulate.”

Do not substitute a ClassicHip survivorship number for an Apex claim. The products are different, and surgeons will notice.

Slide 5 — Close

The ask is simple: identify the right surgeon and the right patient profile, lead with stability, wear performance at the validated test condition, and KinetiCoat fixation advantages. Be confident, be specific, and stay within the approved language.

If a question goes beyond the materials in the field guide, do not improvise. Send it to Product Marketing or Clinical Affairs and we will get an answer back quickly.

MEMORANDUM

TO: Owen Park, CFO; Hannah Berg, FP&A Manager; Dana Okonkwo, VP Regulatory Affairs
FROM: Greg Novak, Director, Post-Market Surveillance
DATE: December 2, 2022
SUBJECT: Registry Trend Update for Reserve Modeling (ApexHip)

Owen and Hannah,

Per our discussion following the Q3 close and Dana’s request for aligned surveillance figures, this memorandum summarizes updated post-market registry metrics for ApexHip to assist FP&A in calibrating future liability reserve modeling.

1. Current Registry Signal Summary

Data captured through the recent 2022 UK National Joint Registry (NJR) cycle and latest American Joint Replacement Registry (AJRR) extracts confirms that the early revision divergence observed in 2021 has not attenuated over time:

* NJR 5-Year Cumulative Revision Rate: ApexHip remains at 7.1% (95% CI: 6.4%–7.9%), compared to the contemporary MoM/cementless class benchmark of 3.2%. The hazard ratio for all-cause revision relative to control hips remains sustained past 48 months post-implantation.
* AJRR Registry Data: US data demonstrates consistent upward trending in primary-to-revision conversions, tracking primarily under diagnostic coding for ARMD, pseudotumor presentation, and unexplained pain with elevated serum cobalt/chromium ion titers.

As a reminder, this represents the continuation of the empirical data set that formed the baseline for our September 14, 2021 Registry Signal Review meeting, during which the committee evaluated withdrawal versus commercial continuation with labeling updates.

2. Correlation with Surgeon Communications and Field Signals

In cross-referencing our post-market complaint tracking against commercial distribution lists, there is a distinct correlation between incoming legal/clinical claim inquiries and clinical sites that received the October 2021 Dear Doctor notification. High-volume implanting centers whose surgeons were directly notified of the high cup inclination angle sensitivity appear to have accelerated patient workups (specifically ordering baseline serum Co/Cr testing and cross-sectional metal-artifact reduction MRIs).

3. Recommendation for Reserve Horizon

Given that the underlying revision trajectory has not flattened, and taking into account the lag between initial radiographic/serological workups and operative revision, I recommend that finance’s forecasting model not assume early stabilization.

Specifically, reserve modeling should anticipate claim volume continuing to rise steadily through FY2023 and into FY2024 before peaking. Assuming revision velocity mirrors historical NJR survival curves for similar large-head MoM bearings, explant rates will persist above market averages across the remaining implanted base.

Please let me know if you require raw data extracts or survival curve stratifications by cup diameter.

VERIDIAN ORTHOPEDICS, INC.
MEMORANDUM

To: Dana Okonkwo, VP Regulatory Affairs
From: Priya Raman, Director, Quality & Complaint Handling
Date: June 30, 2020
Subject: ApexHip Complaint Trending Report - H1 2020

This memorandum summarizes ApexHip complaint activity entered in TrackWise from January 1 through June 30, 2020. The review was conducted per the approved complaint trending procedure and includes complaints received from direct customer contacts, sales representatives, distributors, and surgeon offices. Duplicate reports concerning the same patient event were consolidated where identified.

A total of 68 ApexHip complaints were logged during H1 2020. Of these, 31 complaints relate to elevated cobalt and/or chromium ion values, suspected adverse reaction to metal debris (ARMD), unexplained pain with metal-on-metal bearing concerns, or imaging findings that may be consistent with local tissue reaction. This compares with 19 complaints in the corresponding H1 2019 period.

The increase is notable, although several of the 2020 reports concern implants placed in 2017 and 2018 and therefore reflect a growing population of implants with longer follow-up. The reports are geographically dispersed, with no single account or surgeon responsible for a majority of the entries. Atlanta remains a higher-volume source of reports, but this is not materially different from its overall Apex utilization.

Lot review was completed for complaints where component lot information was available. The implicated cups, stems, and heads span multiple manufacturing periods and component lots. No individual cup lot, stem lot, or head lot represents a meaningful concentration of the metal-ion/ARMD-related complaints. In particular, there is no repeated lot pattern that would support a discrete manufacturing containment action at this time. The current distribution is more consistent with a wear-related or use-condition-related pattern than with a single manufacturing-related event. This conclusion should remain provisional pending receipt of additional implant and surgical-positioning information.

Nine events in the H1 population involve confirmed revision surgery. Explant analysis has been completed or preliminarily reviewed for seven of those cases; the remaining two explants are either with the hospital pathology department or pending return to Veridian. The available analyses describe polished wear areas, linear or arcuate surface scars, and in several cases damage patterns at the cup rim/head interface. Where operative records and radiographs were provided, the cases generally involved higher reported cup inclination angles.

These observations are consistent with the elevated-angle wear concern previously identified in the 2019 engineering re-analysis. As discussed at the time, the standard test configuration did not evaluate all surgical orientations observed in clinical practice. Quality is not making a causal determination based on complaint data alone; however, the alignment between the explant observations and the prior wear-test findings warrants continued close monitoring.

MDR assessments have been completed for all reportable events received through the reporting cutoff. Required submissions have been made within the applicable timelines, and the MDR log is current as of June 30. A small number of files remain open for follow-up medical records and device-return information, but no reportable event is presently overdue for evaluation or filing.

Recommended actions are as follows:

1. Continue monthly ApexHip complaint trending, with a separate review of metal-ion, ARMD, and revision events.
2. Maintain enhanced follow-up requests for radiographs, cup inclination information, metal-ion laboratory values, and explant returns.
3. Provide the updated trend data to Post-Market Surveillance for comparison against available registry data.
4. Reassess whether escalation to a formal cross-functional signal review is appropriate if the current reporting rate continues through Q3.

Legal has been informally briefed regarding the volume increase and the nature of the allegations. No change to the current complaint-handling procedure is proposed at this time.

Priya

4400 Silver Lake Blvd
Warsaw, Indiana 46580

July 2, 2021

Food and Drug Administration
Office of Regulatory Affairs
Detroit District Office
Attn: Investigator R. Delgado
300 River Place, Suite 5900
Detroit, MI 48207

Subject: Response to Form FDA 483, Warsaw, Indiana Facility (FEI: 1834921)
Inspection Dates: June 7 – June 18, 2021

Dear Investigator Delgado:

Veridian Orthopedics, Inc. ("Veridian") submits this formal response to the Form FDA 483 issued on June 18, 2021, at the conclusion of the inspection of our manufacturing facility located at 4400 Silver Lake Blvd, Warsaw, Indiana. Veridian is committed to maintaining full compliance with the Quality System Regulation set forth in 21 CFR Part 820.

We have conducted a thorough review of the three observations cited and are taking immediate corrective and preventive actions, as detailed below.

Observation 1: Procedures for design validation did not adequately ensure that devices conform to defined user needs and intended uses, specifically regarding verification of packaging integrity under extreme temperature storage cycles.
Corrective Action: Packaging engineering has initiated Protocol VAL-2021-088 to re-validate barrier seals under expanded environmental stress ranges. Completion target: August 15, 2021.

Observation 2: Procedures for receiving, reviewing, and evaluating complaints were not adequately maintained to ensure timely statistical trending and analysis, per 21 CFR 820.198 and 21 CFR 820.100. Specifically, during the inspection, the Agency reviewed 142 post-market complaints entered into TrackWise for the ApexHip Total Hip System between Q1 2020 and Q1 2021, noting that statistical trending for adverse tissue reaction events was compiled on an aggregate quarterly cycle rather than at an interval sufficient to detect statistical shifts in a timely manner.
Corrective Action:
1. Veridian is updating standard operating procedure SOP-QA-114 (*Post-Market Surveillance and Complaint Trending*) under Change Order ECO-2021-0412. The revised procedure transitions the formal statistical review cycle for all Class III and implantable reconstructive product lines, specifically including the ApexHip system, from a quarterly to a monthly cadence.
2. The Quality Assurance group will implement automated monthly alert thresholds within TrackWise to flag adverse tissue reaction and metal-ion complaint clusters prior to monthly review meetings.
3. Complaint-handling specialists and post-market surveillance staff will complete comprehensive retraining on SOP-QA-114 by September 17, 2021.

Observation 3: Document control procedures were not consistently followed regarding documentation of training effectiveness verifications in the Agile PLM system.
Corrective Action: Internal QA audit completed on June 28, 2021; administrative workflow updated to mandate supervisor sign-off prior to task execution.

We respectfully request that this response and the planned corrective actions be incorporated into the establishment inspection report.

Sincerely,

Dana Okonkwo
Vice President, Regulatory Affairs
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.

AUDIT COMMITTEE MINUTES

Date: January 21, 2020
Time: 9:00 a.m.–10:05 a.m.
Location: Silver Lake Conference Room, Warsaw, Indiana

Prepared by: Rachel Steinberg, General Counsel

Attendees: Rob Castellano, Owen Park, Dr. Leon Adeyemi, Marcus Lee, Dana Okonkwo
Also Present: Hannah Berg, Financial Planning & Analysis; Michael Dorsey, Internal Audit

1. Call to Order

Mr. Castellano called the meeting to order at 9:00 a.m. The Committee reviewed and approved the minutes from the October 2019 meeting without revision.

2. 2020 Internal Audit Plan

Mr. Dorsey presented the proposed annual internal audit plan. The plan was developed using the company’s enterprise risk assessment, prior audit findings, management interviews, and changes in business operations during 2019.

The proposed plan includes the following principal reviews:

• Procurement controls. Internal Audit will review vendor onboarding, purchase-order approval thresholds, segregation of duties, sole-source documentation, and compliance with the company’s competitive-bid requirements. Management noted that the review should include a sampling of indirect-spend vendors and consulting arrangements.

• IT access management. The audit will assess user provisioning and deprovisioning, periodic access recertifications, administrator access, password settings, and controls surrounding key financial and operational systems. Mr. Park requested particular attention to timely removal of access following employee transfers and separations.

• Expense reporting compliance. Internal Audit will test Concur submissions for required receipts, business-purpose descriptions, approval routing, travel-policy compliance, and duplicate or late-filed expenses. Mr. Lee asked that the review provide practical feedback to field personnel rather than create unnecessary administrative burden.

Additional planned work includes follow-up testing on prior-year findings, quarterly review of the internal audit issue tracker, and an assessment of the company’s vendor master-file controls.

3. Reporting and Timing

Internal Audit will provide status updates at each regularly scheduled Committee meeting and promptly escalate any significant control deficiency. The procurement review is planned for the first quarter, IT access management for the second quarter, and expense reporting compliance for the third quarter.

4. Action Items

Mr. Dorsey will circulate the final 2020 audit calendar and engagement scopes by January 31. Management will identify points of contact for each review and confirm availability of requested records.

There being no further business, the meeting adjourned at 10:05 a.m.

Rachel Steinberg
Secretary to the Audit Committee

FDA Recall Number: Z-1418-2022

Dear Risk Management Colleague:

This letter serves as formal notification that Veridian Orthopedics, Inc. is voluntarily recalling ApexHip acetabular cup lots V-2200 through V-2299, manufactured at our Cork, Ireland facility between November 2021 and February 2022. This action has been classified by FDA as a Class II recall under recall number Z-1418-2022.

This recall was initiated after incoming inspection at two hospital sites identified flaking of the KinetiCoat porous titanium coating upon unwrapping of the sterile package, prior to implantation. Our investigation determined that a plasma-spray process parameter drift, following a chamber maintenance event, resulted in inconsistent coating adhesion in the affected lots. To date, 1,140 units from these lots have been distributed, with approximately 412 implanted.

We are asking that Northgate Health System take the following actions immediately:

1. Identify and quarantine all remaining unimplanted units from lots V-2200 through V-2299 in your inventory.
2. Do not use quarantined units for surgical procedures.
3. Complete the enclosed Effectiveness Check Response Form, documenting your inventory review, and return it to our Regulatory Affairs department within 10 business days of the date of this letter.
4. Contact your Veridian sales representative or Customer Quality at 1-800-555-0142 to arrange return and replacement of quarantined stock at no cost.

If any implanted patients have experienced adverse events potentially related to coating integrity, please report these through your standard adverse event process and notify our Complaint Handling department as well.

We regret any disruption this may cause and appreciate your prompt cooperation. Please contact me directly with any questions.

ENGINEERING MEMORANDUM

Date: March 10, 2022
From: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
Subject: Explant analysis summary - Whitaker case, lot V-2114

This memo summarizes Engineering’s visual and materials review of the retrieved ApexHip femoral head and acetabular cup from the revision performed by Dr. James Whitaker in Denver. The components were received at Warsaw on February 28, 2022, under return authorization RA-22-0317. The cup is identified as lot V-2114. Component identifiers on the returned head are consistent with the operative record supplied by Dr. Whitaker’s office.

The case materials indicate revision after persistent pain, elevated serum cobalt and chromium values, and imaging findings described by the treating team as concerning for an adverse local tissue reaction. I am not making a clinical determination from the device examination; that remains for the treating physician and Clinical/Quality. The observations below are limited to the returned components and associated debris sample.

Visual examination of the bearing surfaces found circumferential polishing on the femoral head, with the more pronounced damage localized to a band corresponding to the superior-lateral cup rim. The cup bearing surface has directional wear striations extending inward from the rim at approximately the 11 to 2 o’clock positions when oriented to the surgeon’s orientation marks. There is also a narrow area of matte discoloration and scratching at the rim transition. The pattern is not consistent with uniform, concentric articulation under nominal orientation.

The available postoperative radiograph supplied with the case file appears to place the cup at a relatively high inclination angle. Exact measurement should be confirmed by Clinical or the treating site, but the apparent orientation is in the range where edge contact becomes more likely.

This is materially similar to the pattern we saw in the 2019 55-degree inclination reruns. In that work, once the contact patch migrated toward the cup rim, wear increased substantially and the resulting head/cup surface damage was directional rather than evenly distributed. The retrieved surfaces here show the same basic mechanism: rim contact/edge loading followed by localized abrasive wear.

Materials analysis of the collected particulate residue identified cobalt/chromium-containing debris. Quantitation from the digestion sample was 18.6 µg cobalt and 7.9 µg chromium per gram of recovered residue. Those values should not be read as a direct measure of total in vivo burden, given recovery limitations and handling at revision, but the composition and relative concentration are consistent with the elevated serum ion readings reported in the case materials.

No coating delamination was observed on the accessible KinetiCoat exterior surface, and this does not appear related to the Cork coating issue associated with the V-2200 series lots. V-2114 is outside that population.

My conclusion is that the retrieval findings are consistent with the known edge-loading wear mechanism at high cup inclination, with associated Co/Cr debris generation. Quality should add this case to the cumulative metal-ion complaint dataset and include it in the next MDR trending review. I recommend retaining the components and microscopy images with the complaint file; Engineering has retained the raw photos and measurement worksheet in the Apex retrieval folder.

Tom Halvorsen
Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip

Date: July 14, 2020
Prepared by: Marcus Lee, VP Sales, Reconstructive
For: Regional Sales Leadership
Subject: Q3 Sales Kickoff - Talking Points Draft

These are draft notes for the regional sessions. Keep the energy up. We had a strong first half in a difficult environment, and the field needs to hear that we are still playing offense. Do not read these word-for-word; use your own voice and make it practical for the reps.

SLIDE 1 — OPENING / WHY WE WIN
“Active adults deserve an active life.” That is the through-line for Apex. The patient is not asking to slow down at 52 because they had a hip replacement. They want confidence getting back to work, golf, travel, family, whatever active means to them.

We are not selling a component in a tray. We are bringing surgeons an option designed around the expectations of a more active patient population.

SLIDE 2 — THE APEX CONVERSATION
Lead with the things surgeons can see in the construct:

• Large head diameter for stability
• A system built for active adults
• A differentiated metal-on-metal platform
• Veridian support before, during, and after the case

If a surgeon raises dislocation risk versus a competitor implant, do not get dragged into a generic implant-versus-implant argument. Bring it back to the large head diameter and stability. “Doctor, one reason surgeons consider Apex for the right active patient is the stability profile associated with the larger head options.” Keep it clinical, keep it simple, and let the surgeon make the patient-selection decision.

SLIDE 3 — POSITIONING DISCIPLINE
We need one story in every region. No freelancing with old leave-behinds, no “lifetime” language, and no numbers that are not in current approved materials. The approved platform is designed for durability, designed for movement, designed for active adults.

SLIDE 4 — QUESTIONS ON REVISIONS
You will get this question, especially from surgeons who follow registry discussions or have been approached by a competitor.

Suggested response: “ApexHip was designed for durability in active adults, and Veridian continues to stand behind the system with surgeon education and clinical support. Patient selection, component positioning, and surgical technique remain important considerations in every total hip.”

Do not quote specific revision statistics in the field. Do not debate a surgeon’s data source. If they want a detailed clinical discussion, involve Medical Affairs or send the question up through your manager. The goal is not to win an argument in the hallway; it is to keep the conversation focused on the appropriate patient and the value of the Apex platform.

SLIDE 5 — CLOSE
Make the ask. Get the evaluation. Support the first cases. Let’s go.

This is the engineering readiness check for the KneeFlex October launch. The Warsaw machining cell tooling has completed the required production-equivalent runs for the primary femoral component sizes. The polyethylene insert mold qualification is also complete. We did see a cosmetic flash condition on three pieces during the second run, but this was corrected by adjusting clamp-force settings. The follow-up run produced acceptable parts. Quality has confirmed that the adjustment does not require a design change or revised acceptance criteria.

Finished-goods inventory is tracking slightly behind the original September plan for the two most commonly forecasted tibial tray sizes. Production lost approximately one shift during the preventive maintenance work on Line 3. Operations’ recovery plan is reasonable: additional weekend production is scheduled for October 5 and 12, and current inventory plus work in process should support the initial launch allocation.

Engineering will maintain a daily review of launch-related technical questions for the first two weeks after release. The launch kit should include the current instrument setup guide, the final surgical technique, and the instrument-tray configuration sheet. Headline finding: lots V-2050 through V-2140 account for the largest concentration of open metal-ion complaints — 64 open cases across that range, which is more than any other lot band we've tracked to date. Average time-to-revision for that group is 3.1 years, which lines up with the wear progression curve Tom described in his 2019 memo on edge-loading at higher inclination angles. I don't see anything in the lot history for V-2050–V-2140 suggesting a coating or process anomaly at the Cork line — no adhesion flags, no plasma-spray deviations noted in the batch records for that window. So per my read this is consistent with the wear mechanism issue Tom flagged, not a manufacturing defect pattern, and it's a distinct population from anything we'd expect to see later out of the V-2200 series (that range hasn't shipped in volume yet so there isn't a comparable complaint base to check against).

Let me know if you want me to break Tab 1 out further by inclination angle where we have post-op imaging data — I know that's been a recurring ask from your side. Happy to hop on a call Monday if useful.

Priya

From: Hannah Berg, Financial Planning & Analysis Manager
To: Reconstructive Segment Distribution List
Subject: Q1 2024 Variance Commentary — Reconstructive Segment

1. Purpose

This memo summarizes Q1 2024 actuals versus the FY2024 budget (approved Nov 2023) for the Reconstructive segment, covering KneeFlex, ClassicHip, and ApexHip product lines. Note that Q1 actuals reflect January and February only for Apex given the timing noted below; March close figures for the rest of the segment are still preliminary pending final Concur T&E allocations, but volume and revenue numbers are locked.

2. KneeFlex

KneeFlex continues to outperform. Units shipped were up 12% year-over-year, driven primarily by continued conversion share gains in the Denver and Dallas territories and a strong response to the revised instrument tray bundling that Sales rolled out in Q4. Revenue growth tracked slightly ahead of unit growth (13.4%) on modest favorable mix toward the larger revision-compatible sizes. ASPs were roughly flat versus budget. We did not see any material pull-forward effect from Q4 promotional pricing, which is encouraging — the growth looks organic rather than borrowed. Marcus's team is forecasting continued double-digit growth through Q2, though I'd treat that with the usual grain of salt until we see April bookings.

3. ClassicHip

ClassicHip wind-down is proceeding essentially on plan. Unit volume declined 22% year-over-year, consistent with the phase-out schedule Product Management laid out last fall. Revenue decline was somewhat steeper than unit decline (-27%) due to unfavorable size mix as remaining inventory skews toward smaller, lower-ASP configurations. No surprises here; this line is winding down as designed and requires no further commentary this quarter.

4. ApexHip

ApexHip revenue was $1.2M in January, already well below the monthly budget run-rate of roughly $7.9M, reflecting the sales slowdown that had been underway since late 2023. Following the voluntary market withdrawal announced February 2, 2024, Apex revenue for February and March was zero. This is the primary driver of the segment-level miss discussed below. The withdrawal was accompanied by an increase to the Apex-related claims reserve, which is reflected in segment operating income but not in the revenue variance itself; Owen's team is handling the reserve mechanics separately and I'd defer to Finance/Legal for specifics on the reserve true-up. From a pure top-line perspective, Apex essentially contributed one month of meaningfully reduced revenue and two months of nothing, versus a budget that assumed continued, if softening, sales through the full quarter.

5. Segment Summary

Combining the three lines, total Reconstructive segment revenue came in 14% below budget for Q1. KneeFlex growth and the planned ClassicHip decline roughly offset each other relative to plan; the entirety of the miss is attributable to the Apex shortfall described above. Absent Apex, the segment would have been within 1–2% of budget.

6. Next Steps

I'll circulate the full variance workbook (Q1_2024_Recon_Variance.xlsx) by end of week. Please flag any line items that look off before we finalize for the March ops review.

Hannah

DESIGN REVIEW MINUTES: DR-3
ApexHip Total Hip System — Wear Testing Protocol & Verification Planning
Document Ref: DHF-0042-M03
Date: November 4, 2016
Location: Warsaw Hub, Conference Room B (and via teleconference)

Attendees:
*   Tom Halvorsen, Lead Design Engineer (ApexHip)
*   Priya Raman, Director, Quality Assurance & Complaint Handling
*   Carlos Mendes, Product Manager (ApexHip)
*   Dana Okonkwo, VP Regulatory Affairs

1. Purpose of Review
The primary objective of this DR-3 milestone was to review and formally baseline the design verification testing protocol for the ApexHip acetabular cup and femoral head articulation, specifically the simulator wear testing matrix required for the planned 510(k) premarket notification.

2. Discussion & Protocol Determination
*   Standard Wear Testing (ISO 14242):
    The team reviewed the standard multi-station hip simulator wear-test protocol under ISO 14242-1 (standard loading cycle, standard 45° nominal inclination angle). Meridian Testing Labs submitted an estimate for a 5-million-cycle run across six test stations and two soak controls.

*   Proposed Extended Edge-Loading / Steep Angle Simulation:
    T. Halvorsen raised a technical proposal to expand the simulator test protocol to evaluate cups under adverse placement angles, specifically adding a secondary cohort tested at a 55° inclination angle to model surgical variance and potential rim loading/micro-separation.

    C. Mendes and D. Okonkwo noted that clearing the 510(k) pathway (predicate: ClassicHip) relies on demonstrating substantial equivalence under recognized consensus standards. D. Okonkwo confirmed that FDA CDRH guidance specifies compliance with ISO 14242 at standard 45° alignment. Running additional simulator banks at 55° would add approximately $140,000 in testing expenses, require securing additional test stations at Meridian, and impose an estimated 16-to-20-week delay on data generation.

    C. Mendes emphasized that market launch expectations require submission in early Q1 2017 to meet commercial rollout targets. Running an expanded non-standard protocol was deemed out of scope and cost-prohibitive given the current development schedule. The review committee concluded that testing at the standard 45° inclination angle alone satisfies design inputs and regulatory predicate expectations. The 55° protocol variation was formally rejected for the DR-3 phase gate.

*   Coating Adhesion Testing (KinetiCoat):
    Per T. Halvorsen’s prior design input memo regarding KBT integration, static shear and tensile adhesion testing (ASTM F1147 / ASTM F1978) for the porous titanium KinetiCoat layer was formally incorporated into the Master Verification Test Plan.

3. Action Items

| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| 1 | Finalize ApexHip Design Verification Plan (DVP-011) reflecting ISO 14242 wear test at standard 45° inclination. | T. Halvorsen | 2016-11-11 |
| 2 | Execute contract work order and package sample lot components for shipment to Meridian Testing Labs. | T. Halvorsen | 2016-11-18 |
| 3 | Align 510(k) predicate testing summary structure with draft Meridian test output format. | D. Mitchell / D. Okonkwo | 2016-12-02 |

MEMORANDUM

TO: Priya Raman, Director of Quality & Complaint Handling; Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip
FROM: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
DATE: January 10, 2022
SUBJECT: Engineering Status Review: ECO-2019-118 (Apex Acetabular Cup Rim Geometry & Clearance) — Closing the Loop

I am writing to formally revisit the open engineering posture surrounding ECO-2019-118. It has now been nearly three years since I submitted the initial Engineering Change Order proposal in February 2019, and our Design History File (DHF) index still does not accurately capture where we stand on this.

To recap the technical history: during the development phase leading up to Design Review 3 (DR-3) in November 2016, our wear simulator protocol was established strictly under ISO 14242-1 standard parameters, testing acetabular component placement at a nominal 45° inclination angle only. The Meridian Testing Labs reports confirmed acceptable volumetric wear under those ideal, nominal conditions, which supported our 510(k) clearance (K162447). However, as I flagged in my February 2019 re-analysis memo, testing the system under steeper acetabular cup inclinations—specifically 55°—produced severe edge-loading dynamics. The wear simulator data showed a 4× to 6× increase in gravimetric and volumetric metal wear rates compared to the 45° baseline, driven by localized contact stresses at the cup rim during microseparation cycles.

ECO-2019-118 proposed an immediate modification to the acetabular rim radius and polar clearance profile to mitigate edge-loading wear at non-ideal cup angles (which clinical data shows occur frequently in real-world patient anatomy).

In mid-2019, leadership decided to formally defer ECO-2019-118. The stated rationale at the time centered on commercial friction: tooling changeout costs, scrap write-downs, and especially the timeline required for full mechanical and simulator requalification, which would have disrupted peak production volumes.

Here is my primary concern today: as of January 2022, three full years after we identified the 4–6× wear multiplier under steep angles, no design change has been implemented. None. The product currently being shipped from Warsaw and Cork retains the exact rim geometry cleared in 2017.

Furthermore, I reviewed the ApexHip DHF index in Agile last week and noticed ECO-2019-118 is marked as "Closed / Superseded by Commercial Labeling Review." This is factually incorrect and creates an audit vulnerability. The engineering risk was never resolved or designed out; it was *deferred*. We should not be relying solely on post-market technique guides or surgeon education to manage a mechanical wear condition that we know occurs once the cup tilts past 50°.

I recommend two immediate corrective actions:
1. Re-open the DHF index entry for ECO-2019-118 and formally designate its status as "Deferred — Pending Clinical Registry / Post-Market Review," explicitly noting that the original ISO 14242 protocol tested only 45° inclination and did not evaluate edge-loading conditions.
2. Reconvene the cross-functional engineering review team (Quality, Product Management, R&D) to decide whether we are going to requalify the modified rim tooling or leave the deferred status on the permanent record.

We have known about the edge-loading wear multiplier since early 2019. Leaving the change order in administrative limbo without a clear engineering resolution is a significant unaddressed risk.

Regards,

Tom Halvorsen
Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.

MEMORANDUM

Date: June 22, 2015
From: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer
To: Priya Raman; Carlos Mendes
Subject: ApexHip concept design kickoff notes

Priya, Carlos —

putting down some notes from the concept kickoff last week so we have a starting point before design inputs get locked. this is early, still moving fast, expect changes.

Basic concept: total hip system, Co/Cr femoral head and stem (same alloy family as ClassicHip, proven manufacturing route), paired with an acetabular cup using the new titanium porous coating we picked up in the KBT deal. calling it KinetiCoat internally for now unless marketing wants something else (carlos - your call). the coating is the differentiator here, better bone ingrowth than our current sintered bead surface, that's the whole pitch for going metal-on-metal with this generation.

Target design inputs, draft:

- head diameters: 36mm to 50mm, in 2mm increments. larger heads for stability/ROM, which is a selling point for the "active" patient segment we keep talking about.
- cup sizes: 44mm to 62mm, matching head range plus offset options
- wear rate target: below ClassicHip benchmark (we'll pull the actual number from the ClassicHip DHF, I think Priya has that on file, need the polyethylene wear data as our comparator even though we're going MoM here, different failure mode obviously but leadership wants an apples-to-apples number for the design input doc)
- inclination range for cup placement: still nailing this down, but leaning toward specifying the standard 40-45 degree range surgeons are trained on. more on that below.

Open item — wear test protocol: we haven't picked a standard yet. ISO 14242 is the obvious baseline, that's what everybody uses and what FDA will expect to see referenced. question is whether we test at a single inclination angle or run a matrix across angles to see how sensitive the wear rate is to cup positioning in the OR, since surgeons don't all hit the same angle every time. I lean toward doing at least a sensitivity check but that adds time and cost to the test campaign. want to get Priya's read on this from a quality/DHF standpoint before I bring it to DR-2.

Timeline: aiming to have design inputs finalized and formally approved by September 2015. That gives us runway to hit DR-3 later this year for the wear test protocol decision and start locking down the coating spec with the KBT engineers (their due diligence notes mentioned they don't have a ton of long-term adhesion data yet, so we'll want to build that into our own verification plan rather than just leaning on their historical data).

Carlos — will need your input on head/cup size matrix vs. what sales thinks the market wants, and whether 50mm heads are overkill or a selling point.

Let's grab 30 min next week to align before I write this up formally.

Tom

Priya, Dana—

Attached is the draft ECO for the Apex cup geometry change we discussed after the 55-degree work.

The proposal is to modify the rim/coverage geometry to give us more tolerance before the head starts riding the edge at higher inclination. The Meridian repeat runs and our internal re-analysis are directionally consistent: at 55° we are seeing roughly 4–6x the wear from the standard 45° setup. This is not a subtle result, even if the standard protocol is technically what was approved in DR-3.

I also referenced the complaint count in the rationale. We do not have every explant or ion result back, but the Atlanta cluster plus the newer entries are enough that I don't think we should treat the test finding as purely theoretical. Priya, please check my wording against the current TrackWise totals/procedure. I used “growing number of complaints involving elevated metal ions, pain, and early revision” rather than a specific number.

This is a real design change, not a drawing cleanup. It would require design verification, wear testing at the revised geometry, risk-file updates, and regulatory assessment before release. My estimate is 9–12 months to implementation if we start now and do not run into another test iteration.

I know the obvious question is whether leadership wants to spend that money versus continuing to monitor complaints and work through labeling/field guidance. That is their call, but I wanted the engineering option documented rather than leaving this as an email discussion.

Attachment: ECO-2019-118_draft.pdf

Tom

CC: Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip; Dana Okonkwo, VP Regulatory Affairs; Dr. Leon Adeyemi, Chief Medical Officer

1. Purpose & Administrative Routing

This memorandum establishes the formal Claim Substantiation File (CSF-2017-004) for all promotional assets supporting the commercial introduction of the ApexHip Total Hip System at the April 2017 National Sales Kickoff in Dallas, Texas.

Per SOP-MKT-302 (*Promotional Material Review and Approval*), all collateral including sales visual aids, detail sheets, patient education booklets, and digital properties managed via Kessler Reid must trace every explicit and implicit product performance claim to verifiable engineering reports, clinical literature, or validated pre-clinical bench testing. Final collateral assets will be cataloged within the Agile PLM environment under change order ECO-2017-088.

2. General Regulatory Guidance

Following discussions with Regulatory Affairs (D. Okonkwo), teams are reminded that FDA 510(k) clearance (K162447, issued March 9, 2017) confirms substantial equivalence to the predicate device (ClassicHip) for commercial distribution purposes only. Under no circumstances should promotional text cite the 510(k) clearance letter as affirmative clinical evidence of safety, superiority, or long-term therapeutic efficacy. All field representatives and marketing agency partners must adhere strictly to cleared indications for use.

3. Promotional Claim Inventory and Substantiation Table

The following claims have been compiled from the primary launch brochure (P/N 093-4011) and the unbranded patient portal preview:

| Claim Text | Promotional Context | Primary Source Document | Review Status / Owner |

VERIDIAN ORTHOPEDICS, INC.
CHANGE CONTROL BOARD — MEETING MINUTES

Meeting: ECO-2019-118 Review (ApexHip Acetabular Cup Rim Geometry)
Date: April 2, 2019
Time: 10:00–11:15 AM
Location: Warsaw HQ, Building 2, Engineering Conference Room
Recorded by: Tom Halvorsen

Attendees: Tom Halvorsen (Sr. Design Engineer), Priya Raman (Director, Quality & Complaint Handling), Carlos Mendes (Product Manager, ApexHip), Devon Mitchell (Sr. Regulatory Specialist), Dana Okonkwo (VP Regulatory Affairs)

1. Background
Halvorsen presented the February 2019 wear-test re-analysis showing 4–6x increased wear rates at 55-degree cup inclination compared to the 45-degree standard used in the original ISO 14242 protocol (DR-3, Nov 2016). ECO-2019-118 was opened to evaluate a proposed rim geometry modification intended to reduce edge-loading wear at higher inclination angles.

2. Discussion
Halvorsen summarized the Meridian Labs data supporting the wear increase and noted the change would require re-tooling of the cup mold and a new round of bench testing, estimated at 4–6 months and roughly $650K in NRE. Mitchell raised the question of whether the change would trigger a new 510(k) versus a letter-to-file determination; Okonkwo stated that a geometry change of this nature would likely require a new submission given potential impact on predicate equivalence, adding regulatory timeline risk.

Raman reported that current TrackWise complaint volume for metal-ion-related issues remained low (single-digit cluster from the 2018 Atlanta group, TW-2018-0912 et seq.) and that no clear registry signal had yet emerged domestically. Mendes noted commercial concerns about disrupting the "Active Life" launch momentum and asked whether the wear data reflected real-world inclination angles or worst-case bench conditions only. Halvorsen acknowledged the bench testing used a fixed 55-degree angle chosen to stress-test edge loading and that clinical inclination distribution data was not yet available.

The group discussed cost, regulatory burden, and the absence of a confirmed clinical signal at this time as factors weighing against an immediate design change.

3. Resolution
The Change Control Board voted to DEFER ECO-2019-118. The board found insufficient clinical signal and complaint trend evidence at this time to justify the cost and regulatory risk of the proposed rim geometry change. The board will revisit the decision upon receipt of additional wear data and updated complaint trending.

Vote: 4 in favor of deferral (Raman, Mendes, Mitchell, Okonkwo), 1 opposed (Halvorsen), recommending continued monitoring.

4. Action Items
- Raman to compile a quarterly complaint trend summary for ApexHip metal-ion/wear-related events, due end of Q2 2019.
- Halvorsen to continue informal wear testing at varied inclination angles outside formal ECO scope, results to be shared at next review.
- Mitchell to note deferral rationale in the DHF change log for ECO-2019-118.
- Next review to be scheduled upon receipt of updated data, no later than Q4 2019.

Minutes approved by consensus of attendees present.

MEMORANDUM

Date: January 29, 2024
From: Rob Castellano, Chief Executive Officer
To: Dana Okonkwo; Owen Park; Rachel Steinberg; Dr. Leon Adeyemi; Marcus Lee
Subject: Decision Memo — Voluntary Market Withdrawal of ApexHip

This memo confirms the Board's decision, reached in yesterday's session, to voluntarily withdraw ApexHip from the market effective February 2, 2024. I want to lay out the basis for this decision and assign next steps.

Background. The registry signal on ApexHip's revision rate is not new. The March 2021 NJR annual report first flagged a 5-year revision rate of 7.1% against a class average of 3.2%, a gap AJRR data corroborated later that year. We formally evaluated that signal at the September 14, 2021 Registry Signal Review and made the judgment at the time to continue selling with a labeling update and surgeon communication. That was a reasonable decision on the information available then. It is no longer the right decision.

Since that meeting, the picture has not improved. Dr. Adeyemi's updated clinical assessment, which the Board reviewed this month, concludes that the pattern of ARMD-related revisions is consistent with a durable, product-level issue rather than a surgical-technique or cohort artifact. Separately, the formation of MDL 3102 in December has changed the litigation posture materially, and outside counsel's assessment is that continued marketing in the face of the current registry and clinical record increases both patient risk and legal exposure in ways the Board is not willing to accept.

Taking the registry trend, Dr. Adeyemi's assessment, and the litigation and regulatory environment together, I have decided — with the Board's support — to withdraw ApexHip from the market voluntarily, effective February 2, 2024. This is a market withdrawal, not a recall of implanted devices; existing patients should continue to be managed per standard clinical follow-up, and Dr. Adeyemi's office will issue clinical guidance separately.

Actions:

1. Dana — please finalize FDA notification of the withdrawal and coordinate any related regulatory filings. I'd like the notification submitted no later than February 1.

2. Marcus — please prepare sales force communication so the field organization is aligned before the public announcement. I don't want reps caught flat-footed by customers or press.

3. Owen — please update reserve estimates in light of the withdrawal and loop in Rachel on any disclosure implications.

Rachel, please coordinate the public statement and customer notice language with Marcus and Dana.

I recognize this is a significant step for the company and for the people who have worked on this product since 2015. It is the right one. Please treat the timeline above as firm.

Rob

MEMORANDUM

Date: November 1, 2019
From: Priya Raman, Director, Quality & Complaint Handling
Subject: Complaint Trending Summary — ApexHip Q3 2019
Distribution: D. Okonkwo (VP Regulatory Affairs); T. Halvorsen (Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip)

1. Purpose

This memo summarizes ApexHip complaint trending for Q3 2019 (July–September) per Complaint Handling Procedure QSP-014, and provides a comparison against Q1 and Q2 2019 volumes.

2. Complaint Volume Summary

Total ApexHip complaints logged in TrackWise for Q3 2019: 9. Of these, 4 are classified as suspected metal-ion/wear-related (elevated cobalt/chromium, pain, or suspected ARMD presentation), consistent with the pattern first identified in the Atlanta cluster (TW-2018-0311, TW-2018-0312, TW-2018-0319). No new Atlanta complaints were received this quarter; those three cases remain open pending explant analysis per procedure.

New complaints of note this quarter:

- TW-2019-0402 — Nashville, Dr. A. Rao's practice. Patient presenting with groin pain at 22 months post-implant; elevated serum cobalt reported by treating physician. Investigation ongoing.
- TW-2019-0417 — Denver, reporting surgeon Dr. J. Whitaker. Patient with joint effusion and suspected pseudotumor on imaging; revision surgery scheduled. Explant tissue requested per procedure.

Combined with the three Atlanta cases, this brings open metal-ion-pattern complaints to five as of quarter end, up from three at the close of Q2 2019 and two at the close of Q1 2019. The rate remains a small fraction of total units implanted to date, but the quarter-over-quarter increase warrants continued close monitoring per QSP-014 Section 6.

3. Relationship to Ongoing Engineering Evaluation

Quality is aware of the wear-test re-analysis conducted by T. Halvorsen (memo to P. Raman and C. Mendes, February 2019) identifying increased wear at 55-degree cup inclination relative to the standard 45-degree test condition. While no root-cause determination has been made linking specific complaint cases to inclination angle, Quality considers this analysis a relevant input to trending review and will continue to track complaint data against any engineering conclusions as they develop.

4. Recommendation

Based on current volumes and severity, Quality does not recommend a design change or field action at this time. We recommend:

(a) continued monthly trending review of ApexHip complaints per standard cadence;
(b) a follow-up periodic re-review of the metal-ion-pattern cluster at the close of Q4 2019, incorporating any explant findings from TW-2019-0417 and TW-2019-0402; and
(c) continued coordination with Regulatory Affairs regarding MDR reportability determinations on a case-by-case basis per 21 CFR 803.

Please contact me with questions or corrections prior to filing.

Priya Raman
Director, Quality & Complaint Handling
