MEETING MINUTES

Meeting: Apex Coating Issue Field Action Decision Meeting
Date: April 21, 2022
Time: 10:00–11:15 a.m. ET
Location: Teams / Warsaw Hub, Conference Room 4B
Prepared by: Dana Okonkwo, VP Regulatory Affairs

Attendees: Dana Okonkwo, Priya Raman, Bill Kowalski, Rachel Steinberg, Carlos Mendes, Owen Park

Purpose
To review the KinetiCoat adhesion issue affecting certain ApexHip acetabular cup lots and determine the appropriate field action.

Discussion Summary

Mr. Kowalski reviewed Cork manufacturing records and the preliminary investigation. The affected population is cup lots V-2200 through V-2299, manufactured following the plasma-spray chamber maintenance event. The current evidence supports parameter drift during the relevant production period as the probable cause of insufficient KinetiCoat adhesion. The observed failure mode is coating flaking or separation identified on unwrapping during incoming inspection at two hospital customers.

Ms. Raman confirmed that the distribution reconciliation currently identifies 1,140 affected units distributed. Of those, 412 are recorded as implanted. The remaining units are believed to be in hospital inventory, distributor inventory, or otherwise pending confirmation through the effectiveness process. Quality will continue reconciliation as customer responses are received.

The group agreed that the product should be removed from distribution and that a voluntary Class II recall is warranted for lots V-2200 through V-2299. Regulatory will proceed on that basis, subject to final review of the notification package and lot list.

For avoidance of doubt, the scope of this field action is limited to the KinetiCoat adhesion/manufacturing issue associated with the identified cup lots. Metal-ion levels, wear performance, ARMD, registry data, and other metal-on-metal concerns were expressly noted as outside the scope of this action. Those matters are being addressed through their respective Quality, Post-Market Surveillance, and Regulatory processes and should not be characterized in customer communications as the basis for this recall.

Ms. Okonkwo advised that the target for recall initiation should be mid-June 2022, allowing time for completion of the health hazard evaluation, final lot tracing, customer lists, and FDA notification materials. Ms. Steinberg requested that communications remain factual and limited to the identified coating adhesion condition, the affected lots, and the customer instructions.

Mr. Mendes noted that Sales will require a concise field script and FAQ once the customer letter is approved. Ms. Raman stated that the initial hospital notification should instruct customers to identify, quarantine, and return unused affected cups, while providing a contact path for questions regarding implanted devices. No clinical recommendation language will be included without Regulatory and clinical review.

Mr. Park confirmed that Finance will begin modeling the anticipated reserve, including return logistics, replacement product, customer notification, and potential claim exposure. He asked Quality to provide a weekly update on the distributed/implanted reconciliation.

Action Items

1. Dana Okonkwo — Draft FDA voluntary recall notification, health hazard evaluation, and associated Regulatory package. Target: May 6, 2022.
2. Priya Raman — Prepare hospital notification letter, distribution list, return instructions, and effectiveness-check process. Target: May 13, 2022.
3. Bill Kowalski — Complete Cork batch-record review and provide final affected-lot confirmation and root-cause documentation. Target: April 29, 2022.
4. Owen Park — Begin financial reserve modeling based on 1,140 distributed units and 412 implanted units; update as reconciliation changes. Target: May 6, 2022.
5. Carlos Mendes — Prepare draft Sales FAQ and field communication plan after Quality/Regulatory approve customer language. Target: May 20, 2022.
6. Rachel Steinberg — Review external communications and recall materials before issuance. Target: upon receipt of drafts.

MEMORANDUM

To: Rachel Steinberg, General Counsel; Marcus Lee, VP Sales, Reconstructive
From: Owen Park, Chief Financial Officer
Date: October 2, 2020
Subject: Annual review of KOL compensation spend - Apex program

I have completed Finance’s annual review of the ApexHip key opinion leader and physician-engagement spend through September 30, including the supporting invoices, speaker-program records, travel and expense submissions, and royalty reporting provided by Commercial Operations.

At a program level, the spend remains within the board-approved physician consulting and education budget. Apex continues to be a meaningful growth driver, and the clinical education component remains important to adoption, particularly for surgeons new to the larger-head MoM procedure. That said, the concentration of spend among a small number of physicians is worth continued attention, both from a budget-management standpoint and in light of increasing regulatory scrutiny of device-maker relationships with KOLs industry-wide.

The figures below exclude ordinary customer meals below the company reporting threshold, product evaluation units, and broader professional-society sponsorships. They include amounts processed through Accounts Payable and Concur as of September 30. Q4 estimates are not included.

| Physician / group | Payment category | 2019 Q1–Q4 | 2020 Q1–Q3 | 2019–2020 YTD |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Dr. Marcus Feld | Consulting/design advisory | $82,500 | $61,250 | $143,750 |
| Dr. Marcus Feld | Royalty payments | $32,400 | $20,100 | $52,500 |
| Dr. Marcus Feld | Travel, lodging and meeting expenses | $5,900 | $2,850 | $8,750 |
| Dr. Marcus Feld subtotal |  | $120,800 | $84,200 | $205,000 |
| Dr. Anita Rao | Speaker honoraria | $28,500 | $21,000 | $49,500 |
| Dr. Anita Rao | Travel, lodging and meeting expenses | $4,100 | $4,400 | $8,500 |
| Dr. Anita Rao subtotal |  | $32,600 | $25,400 | $58,000 |
| Four regional surgeons | Case observations / proctoring support | $12,000 | $10,000 | $22,000 |
| Total Apex KOL and physician-engagement spend |  | $165,400 | $119,600 | $285,000 |

The four regional-surgeon arrangements are individually modest and relate primarily to case observation, peer-to-peer education, and feedback following early use of Apex at sites where we were building a reference base. The participating surgeons were Dr. Paul Neri (Dallas), Dr. Allison Kane (Charlotte), Dr. Miguel Santos (Orlando), and Dr. Ethan Brooks (Denver). Payment files generally identify the applicable program and dates of service. A few older files rely on Sales’ event records rather than a standalone engagement summary; those should be cleaned up before any renewal or new work is approved.

Dr. Feld remains the largest individual recipient because he has three distinct relationships with Veridian: design consulting, speaker-program participation, and the royalty arrangement associated with his Apex design contribution. The royalty calculation was reconciled to the underlying agreement and quarterly sales data. Finance did not identify a payment outside the agreement terms. Nevertheless, the cumulative number will attract attention simply because of its size and his visibility in the Apex program. Marcus, please make sure field personnel understand that consulting status does not change the approval process for customer-related expenses, product requests, or speaking engagements.

Dr. Rao’s spend is principally honoraria for approved educational programs, with limited travel associated with advisory-board and faculty activity. Her total is consistent with prior periods and below the annual planning assumption. I note that several 2020 programs moved to virtual delivery, which accounts for the lower travel component but does not eliminate the need for attendance records, agenda support, and documented educational content.

My recommendation is not to reduce the program solely because it is concentrated. Rather, we should tighten the file discipline around fair-market-value determinations and business justification. Specifically:

1. Commercial should retain a current FMV analysis for each consulting, faculty, advisory-board, and case-observation rate, rather than relying on a prior-year rate card without an explicit renewal review.

2. Each engagement should have a short statement of need tied to a defined service: design input, training, case observation, or an approved educational presentation. “Relationship development” is not an adequate description for the file.

3. Travel should be supported by a program agenda and actual attendance or service confirmation. Finance will continue to reject unsupported upgrades, companion travel, and expenses without a clear business purpose.

4. Royalty administration should remain segregated from speaker and consulting approvals. The contracts are different, and the record should make that distinction obvious.

5. Legal and Compliance should confirm that the current Sunshine reporting mapping captures all payment types consistently, including travel booked centrally and expenses reimbursed through Concur.

Rachel, I would appreciate Legal’s view on whether the current consulting-agreement templates and FMV memoranda need updating before the 2021 renewals. Marcus, Commercial Operations should identify the engagement owner for every active Apex physician file by October 30. Finance can provide the underlying transaction listing if helpful, but I would prefer we resolve missing support prospectively rather than reconstruct it at year-end.

The program is within budget and has not created a forecast issue. The more relevant concern is that our records should demonstrate that we are paying for legitimate, defined services at supportable rates, particularly as the industry receives more attention in this area.

Owen

SUBJECT: Workforce Transition Plan - ApexHip Market Withdrawal

Following the February 2, 2024 announcement regarding the voluntary global market withdrawal of the ApexHip Total Hip System, Human Resources has finalized the workforce transition and organizational alignment plan.

While this market action impacts product line revenue and commercial focus, our regulatory, clinical, and quality obligations for previously implanted units remain fully active. Consequently, this plan balances necessary commercial consolidation with targeted personnel retention across technical operations.

1. Scope of Impacted Personnel

The withdrawal directly impacts positions dedicated exclusively to the commercialization, promotional positioning, and field support of ApexHip:

• Commercial Sales: Five (5) Regional Reconstruction Specialists whose sole portfolio assignment was ApexHip conversion accounts across the Southeast, Central, and Western territories. General reconstructive sales representatives carrying KneeFlex and shoulder lines will absorb remaining territory accounts and are unaffected by this reduction.
• Marketing Communications: Four (4) dedicated contractor roles within MarCom supporting Apex product campaigns, digital asset management, and agency liaison work (Kessler Reid deliverables). Contracts will be concluded effective February 29, 2024, per standard notice provisions.
• Operations / Field Inventory: Two (2) logistics coordinator roles in Warsaw supporting hospital consignment retrieval and field kit balancing.

2. Retention of Core Technical, Quality, and Regulatory Staff

It is critical to emphasize that no headcount reductions will occur within Product Development, Regulatory Affairs, Post-Market Surveillance, or Quality Complaint Handling.

Per 21 CFR 820 and 803 requirements, our post-market surveillance, adverse event trending, and complaint investigation responsibilities continue indefinitely for all legacy implanted ApexHip systems. The following teams will remain intact:

• Quality & Complaint Handling: Priya Raman’s team will maintain current staffing levels to manage incoming TrackWise complaint files, MDR determinations, and explant evaluations.
• Post-Market Surveillance: Greg Novak will continue overseeing registry monitoring (AJRR, NJR), signal detection, and ongoing surveillance reports.
• R&D Engineering: Lead sustaining engineer Wei Chen and supporting mechanical testing staff will remain fully allocated to ongoing retrieval analyses, wear simulator evaluations, and technical support for ongoing regulatory inquiries.

3. Severance and Transition Package Terms

For eligible regular full-time employees subject to position elimination, Veridian will offer standard severance packages structured as follows:

• Base Severance: Two (2) weeks of base pay per year of continuous service, with a minimum of eight (8) weeks and a maximum of twenty-six (26) weeks.
• Benefits Continuation: Employer-subsidized COBRA premium coverage corresponding to the severance duration period.
• Incentive Compensation: Pro-rated FY2024 target bonus payouts calculated through March 31, 2024.
• Outplacement Services: Three (3) months of executive and professional outplacement assistance via Lee Hecht Harrison (LHH).

4. Implementation Timeline

• Feb 5–Feb 9: Finalize Workday role status updates; prepare individualized separation documentation and release agreements with outside legal review.
• Feb 12–Feb 16: Manager briefing sessions; coordinate notification scheduling with VP Sales Marcus Lee and relevant regional directors.
• Feb 19–Feb 23: Conduct individual notification meetings with impacted commercial staff.
• Feb 29: Contract conclusion date for MarCom external contractors.
• March 29, 2024: Target final separation date for impacted regular employees.

Please direct any questions regarding specific employee conversations or Workday processing directly to me.

MEMORANDUM

TO: Post-Market Surveillance Committee; Dana Okonkwo, VP Regulatory Affairs; Priya Raman, Director, Quality & Complaint Handling
FROM: Greg Novak, Director, Post-Market Surveillance
DATE: June 1, 2020
SUBJECT: KneeFlex Total Knee System — Post-Market Surveillance Summary (Q2 2020)

1. Purpose & Scope
This memorandum summarizes the routine post-market clinical follow-up and surveillance data for the KneeFlex Total Knee System for the second quarter of 2020, covering cumulative commercial experience from launch (October 2019) through May 15, 2020.

2. Surveillance Methodology
The surveillance protocols applied in this review utilize the standardized Veridian Post-Market Surveillance Registry Integration Protocol (SOP-PMS-042). This methodology mirrors the active surveillance workflows currently deployed across all Veridian reconstructive joint product lines, including our primary hip portfolios (ClassicHip and ApexHip) and ShoulderPro. Specifically, internal complaint intake from TrackWise is cross-indexed against quarterly dataset releases from the American Joint Replacement Registry (AJRR) and regional hospital purchasing registries, applying cumulative incidence estimates and survivorship modeling (Kaplan-Meier analysis).

3. Registry & Complaint Findings
To date, commercial distribution of KneeFlex has reached an estimated 4,820 implanted units across the United States.

- Cumulative Revision Rate: KneeFlex currently demonstrates an all-cause cumulative revision rate of 1.8% at roughly 8 months of follow-up. By comparison, the aggregate AJRR class benchmark for contemporary cruciate-retaining and posterior-stabilized total knee arthroplasty systems stands at 3.2% for equivalent timepoints.
- Primary Revision Drivers: Among the limited verified revisions reported in TrackWise (n=14), primary failure modes are distributed as follows:
  * Infection / Septic Loosening: 8 cases (57.1%)
  * Periprosthetic Fracture (traumatic): 4 cases (28.6%)
  * Instability / Sizing Mismatch: 2 cases (14.3%)
- Mechanical & Wear Metrics: There have been zero reports of tibial insert disassociation, premature polyethylene delamination, or abnormal metallic debris generation.

4. Registry Signals
No statistically significant performance or safety outliers have been detected across any age cohort or patient demographic. The funnel plot analysis for KneeFlex across high-volume participating institutions remains well within the 95% and 99.8% control limits. No registry safety alerts, outlier notices, or external trending inquiries have been issued by AJRR or regulatory bodies regarding this system.

5. Summary & Next Steps
KneeFlex continues to perform exceptionally well in early post-market tracking, tracking comfortably below competitive revision baselines. Standard surveillance will continue per the established schedule, with the next formal registry pull scheduled for September 2020 ahead of the Q3 PMS Committee review. No changes to the Risk Management File, Instructions for Use (IFU), or clinical evaluation plans are recommended at this time.

Date: Wed, 10 Feb 2021 09:41:05 -0500
Subject: RE: Early look at 2021 NJR data ahead of March report

Greg, Dana,

Thank you for flagging this early. A 7.1% five-year revision rate is certainly a figure that will command attention from both the registry steering group and our European surgeons.

We must exercise standard clinical caution before drawing definitive conclusions from aggregate registry data. Revision disparities frequently reflect confounding variables, particularly patient selection criteria (e.g., higher activity profiles in younger cohorts) or variable surgical technique across centers, rather than intrinsic device design flaws alone.

That said, the biomechanical mechanism Tom Halvorsen described regarding micro-separation and edge loading at steeper acetabular cup inclination angles (55°+) is entirely biologically plausible. If high-angle placement generates localized wear stripes and accelerated metal ion release, early adverse local tissue reactions would clinically manifest right around the 3- to 5-year mark.

We should not attempt to dissect this piecemeal. Once the NJR tables are finalized next month, I recommend convening a formal joint Clinical-Regulatory-Quality review meeting to examine the explant data, registry sub-cohorts, and our current IFU.

Best regards,

Leon

Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.

There are clear published parallels to what Greg is tracking in the NJR dataset and the steep wear gradient Tom Halvorsen documented in his 2019 simulator re-analysis at elevated cup abduction angles (>50°). In particular, the clinical community has documented that when steep acetabular inclination induces stripe wear and micro-separation, local tissue necrosis and pseudotumor formation correlate heavily with serum Co and Cr spikes, even before frank mechanical loosening shows up on radiographs.

MEMORANDUM

Date: October 12, 2018
From: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer
Subject: KneeFlex Design FMEA - Rev 1

This memo documents the first formal design FMEA for the KneeFlex tibial insert, tibial tray interface, femoral component, and associated trialing instrumentation. This revision incorporates the bench findings from the August build and the usability observations from the Warsaw cadaver lab. The worksheet is being routed with the Rev 1 design package and will be updated after completion of the fatigue and simulator protocols.

The intent here is to identify reasonably foreseeable component and instrument failures before design verification is locked. Scores use the standard Veridian 1–10 scale for Severity (S), Occurrence (O), and Detection (D). Risk Priority Number (RPN) is S x O x D. Items at or above 120 require a documented mitigation or rationale before the next design review.

| Item / Failure Mode | Potential Effect | S | Potential Cause | O | Current Controls / Detection | D | RPN |
|---|---|---:|---|---:|---|---:|---:|
| Polyethylene tibial insert wear above expected rate | Osteolysis, pain, early revision | 8 | Inadequate resin processing; elevated contact stress in deep flexion | 4 | Resin certification; dimensional inspection; simulator test planned | 5 | 160 |
| Tibial insert locking feature fatigue or disengagement | Insert micromotion, instability, debris generation | 9 | Repeated posterior loading; tolerance stack between insert and tray | 3 | Locking-force test; cyclic fatigue test in development | 5 | 135 |
| Femoral component cementless surface insufficient for fixation | Migration, pain, revision procedure | 9 | Porosity variation; inadequate surface preparation | 3 | Coating thickness inspection; pull-off samples; radiographic migration protocol planned | 4 | 108 |
| Femoral component fracture | Loss of function, revision surgery | 10 | Material defect; undersized component in high-load patient | 1 | Material lot certification; finite element analysis; fatigue test | 4 | 40 |
| Tibial tray post deformation | Insert instability or altered kinematics | 8 | High cyclic load at post base; machining variation | 2 | Dimensional inspection; bench fatigue test | 5 | 80 |
| Trial inserter or extraction instrument breakage | Extended operative time; possible retained fragment | 7 | Instrument shaft overload; repeated reprocessing; improper engagement | 3 | Torque specification; cadaver-lab inspection; instrument fatigue test | 5 | 105 |

The highest initial RPN is insert wear. This is not unexpected for a mobile-bearing-adjacent design, although KneeFlex is a fixed-bearing system. The issue is not the nominal wear result; it is the sensitivity of the design to alignment and to the backside contact pattern if the insert is not fully seated. The current simulator plan includes neutral alignment and a malalignment condition. I recommend adding a deliberately incomplete seating condition to the bench protocol rather than assuming the locking click is sufficient confirmation in all cases. Manufacturing should also retain molding and irradiation records by insert lot for the verification builds.

The locking mechanism is the next item needing work. In the August build, two inserts showed visible witness marking along the anterior rail after repeated removal and reinsertion. Neither disengaged, but the force-to-remove values dropped after the tenth cycle. That may be an artifact of the prototype machining, but we should not treat it as one until the production-intent tray and insert are tested together. The proposed control is to establish a minimum retention force and maximum insertion force specification, then confirm both after cyclic loading.

For the femoral component, the current concern is less fracture than fixation consistency. The porous surface process is still being finalized with Cork, and the coupon data are acceptable but limited. We need production-representative coupons before closing this line item. The severity remains high because a fixation failure is clinically significant even if the expected occurrence is low.

Instrument breakage was raised by two surgeons during the cadaver lab, specifically when the trial extraction tool was used at an angle rather than inline with the tray. The current design has insufficient margin for that use condition. Engineering will evaluate a larger shaft diameter and a revised engagement geometry. Training language alone is not an adequate control if the instrument predictably sees off-axis loading in surgery.

Actions before the next design review:

1. Add incomplete-insert-seating and deep-flexion conditions to the wear and locking verification protocol.
2. Define acceptance criteria for locking retention force following cyclic loading and repeated instrument use.
3. Obtain production-intent coating coupons and process capability information from Cork.
4. Redesign the trial extraction instrument interface and repeat the cadaver-lab evaluation.
5. Re-score the FMEA after verification results are available and document any residual risk rationale.

Tom Halvorsen
Sr. Design Engineer, Knee Reconstruction

Date: January 20, 2021
From: Devon Mitchell, Sr. Regulatory Specialist
To: File / Regulatory Affairs — MDR Tracking
Subject: MDR Filing Summary — Q4 2020 ApexHip Metal-Ion Cases

1. Purpose

This memo summarizes the six individual Medical Device Reports (MDRs) filed with FDA under 21 CFR 803.50 during Q4 2020 involving ApexHip patients with elevated cobalt/chromium levels and subsequent revision surgery.

2. Cases Filed

- TW-2020-0871 — implant 8/2018, revision 10/2020 (26 mo.), elevated Co/Cr, tissue staining noted at revision.
- TW-2020-0902 — implant 3/2019, revision 11/2020 (20 mo.), Co 12.4 ppb, pseudotumor on MRI.
- TW-2020-0915 — implant 1/2018, revision 9/2020 (32 mo.), Co/Cr both elevated, ARMD confirmed histologically.
- TW-2020-0933 — implant 6/2018, revision 12/2020 (30 mo.), metallosis at revision, cup inclination not yet confirmed.
- TW-2020-0947 — implant 11/2018, revision 12/2020 (25 mo.), elevated Cr, patient-reported groin pain preceding revision by ~4 months.
- TW-2020-0958 — implant 2/2019, revision 10/2020 (20 mo.), elevated Co/Cr, ARMD noted intraoperatively.

Each filing was submitted within the applicable 30-day timeframe from the date our complaint-handling group (Priya Raman's team) determined the report met MDR reportability criteria. All six are cross-referenced above to their originating TrackWise records for traceability into the DHF and complaint files.

3. Symptom Onset

Average time from implantation to onset of reported symptoms (pain, swelling, or elevated ion levels prompting workup) across these six cases is approximately 26 months post-implant, consistent with the range observed in prior quarters.

4. Cumulative Trend

Including these six, Veridian has now filed or has pending a cumulative total of 19 MDRs for ApexHip metal-ion/ARMD-related events since the first such report in 2018. This represents a continued increase in filing frequency relative to 2019 quarterly averages, though absolute implant volumes have also grown over the same period.

5. Coordination Note

Dana has asked that this cumulative trend be prepared as a discussion item for the Registry Signal Review group later this year, particularly in light of the NJR annual report expected in March, which we anticipate may include updated revision-rate data for ApexHip. I will begin assembling the case-level detail and a trend chart for that discussion once the NJR figures are available.

6. Distribution

This memo is retained in the Regulatory Affairs MDR tracking file. No further action required at this time beyond routine monitoring of new TrackWise entries meeting reportability criteria.

— Devon Mitchell

MEMORANDUM

TO: Employee Personnel File: Dana Okonkwo (VP, Regulatory Affairs)
FROM: Lisa Tran, HR Business Partner, R&D and Quality
DATE: March 20, 2022
SUBJECT: 2021 Annual Performance Review – Dana Okonkwo

Overall Performance Rating: Exceeds Expectations (4/5)
Review Period: January 1, 2021 – December 31, 2021
Manager / Reviewer: Rob Castellano, Chief Executive Officer (with HR BP concurrence)

Executive Summary

Throughout 2021, Dana Okonkwo consistently demonstrated exceptional regulatory rigor and executive leadership across Veridian Orthopedics' portfolio. As Vice President of Regulatory Affairs, Dana navigated the organization through significant domestic and international compliance challenges, maintaining strong agency relationships while providing disciplined oversight to product lifecycle management.

Key Achievements & Milestone Deliverables

* Management of June 2021 FDA Inspection: Dana led Veridian’s response to the comprehensive FDA facility inspection of the Warsaw Hub in June 2021. Following the issuance of the Form 483 containing three observations (notably including inspection findings regarding complaint trending timeliness under 21 CFR 820.198), Dana coordinated across Quality, Post-Market Surveillance, and Engineering to author and deliver a thorough, defensible response within the statutory timeline in July 2021. Her precise regulatory framing and rapid remediation planning satisfied CDRH concerns and minimized formal escalation risk.
* Registry Signal Review Leadership: In September 2021, following the release of annual registry publications (specifically the UK NJR 5-year dataset indicating elevated revision metrics for the ApexHip metal-on-metal construct), Dana played an indispensable role during the executive Registry Signal Review process. She maintained regulatory objectivity, evaluated European and US surveillance data, and guided leadership to an evidence-backed strategy. This included drafting the targeted labeling update and coordinating the subsequent October 2021 "Dear Doctor" communication to orthopedic surgeons regarding optimal cup positioning and patient monitoring.
* Global Regulatory Maintenance: Maintained timely Medical Device Reporting (MDR) workflows and ensured European Medical Device Regulation (EU MDR) transition milestones stayed largely on schedule across reconstructive product lines, despite considerable resource constraints.

Development Areas & Goals for 2022

* Strategic Delegation: While Dana’s meticulous, detail-oriented approach guarantees regulatory compliance of the highest standard, her direct management style sometimes risks creating a bottleneck on mid-level filings. With Devon Mitchell taking on increased responsibility for MDR maintenance and daily submissions, Dana is encouraged to delegate operational reviews more broadly to empower her senior team and free up capacity for enterprise-level risk mitigation.
* Talent Development: Formalize succession planning and expand specialized training for the Regulatory Affairs team in response to growing PMS audit intensity.

Compensation & Next Steps

RE: Formal Complaint – ApexHip System Early Revision (Patient Ref: RM-7104)

Dear Ms. Raman:

I am writing to file a formal complaint regarding a catastrophic failure of the ApexHip total hip system in a 54-year-old male patient whom I revised last week, exactly 38 months post-index procedure.

The patient presented with severe groin pain, persistent clicking, and joint effusion. Workup revealed markedly elevated metal ions, with serum cobalt measured at 18.7 ppb (chromium was 12.4 ppb). Intraoperatively, upon arthrotomy, I encountered profound metallosis with extensive soft tissue necrosis surrounding the abductor mechanism and a large pseudotumor extending anteriorly. The acetabular cup (54 mm) and femoral head (44 mm) showed obvious eccentric wear bands. The components were stable at the bone interface, but the local tissue destruction was severe enough to require extensive debridement and conversion to a constrained revision construct.

I specifically reviewed the initial postoperative films; cup inclination was 51 degrees, which is well within acceptable clinical placement for active patients. In speaking informally with several regional colleagues over the summer, I understand I am not the only surgeon seeing this pattern. Is Veridian tracking other reports of ARMD and accelerated wear with the ApexHip? Specifically, has your engineering team identified a design issue or edge-loading vulnerability with this cup at higher inclination angles?

Given the severity of the tissue destruction I observed, I expect a prompt and detailed written response regarding whether this event is being investigated under your CAPA system and reported to regulatory authorities. The explanted components have been decontaminated and retained per protocol.

Sincerely,

James Whitaker, MD
Denver Orthopedic Specialists
Attending Orthopedic Surgeon

RECALL EFFECTIVENESS CHECK REPORT — ROUND 2 SUMMARY
FDA Recall Number: Z-1418-2022
Product: ApexHip Acetabular Cup, Lots V-2200 through V-2299

Date: September 12, 2022
Prepared by: Priya Raman, Director, Quality & Complaint Handling
Distribution: Dana Okonkwo (VP Regulatory Affairs); Bill Kowalski (Plant Manager, Cork)

1. PURPOSE

Per procedure QSP-806-04 and the recordkeeping requirements of 21 CFR 806, this report documents the second-round effectiveness check for the voluntary Class II recall initiated June 14, 2022, covering ApexHip acetabular cup lots V-2200–V-2299 (1,140 units distributed).

2. SUMMARY OF FINDINGS

As of the close of the Round 2 verification window (September 9, 2022), field accountability stands as follows:

- Total units distributed: 1,140
- Units accounted for: 1,094 (96.0%)
- Confirmed implanted (per hospital/ASC attestation): 412
- Units returned to Veridian or confirmed destroyed on-site: 682
- Units remaining untraced: 46 (4.0%)

This represents an improvement over the Round 1 check (July 2022), which accounted for approximately 88% of distributed units. Per procedure, a third round is not automatically required once accountability exceeds 95%, but given the number of small accounts still outstanding, I am recommending continued targeted follow-up rather than closing the file at this time.

3. OUTSTANDING UNITS

The 46 untraced units are concentrated at two accounts, both smaller ambulatory surgical centers rather than hospital systems:

- Crestview Ambulatory Surgical Center (approx. 27 units unaccounted)
- Lakeside Same-Day Surgery Center (approx. 19 units unaccounted)

Both accounts received the original June 14 recall notification and a follow-up letter dated July 28. Neither has returned a completed accountability form as of this writing. Field sales (Southeast region) has been asked to assist in obtaining direct confirmation from purchasing/materials management contacts at each site, since phone follow-up from Quality has not been productive.

4. ROOT CAUSE STATUS

Root cause for the coating adhesion nonconformance remains as previously reported: plasma-spray parameter drift following a chamber maintenance event at the Cork facility, affecting the KinetiCoat application process for the subject lot range. This is documented in CAPA-2022-0091, which remains open pending completion of the effectiveness check and closure of associated corrective actions (chamber requalification protocol, revised post-maintenance verification step). Bill, per our last conversation I don't believe there's anything further needed from the Cork line for this report, but please let me know if the CAPA team wants updated batch records referenced here.

5. RECOMMENDATION

I recommend:

(a) Issuing a second follow-up letter to Crestview and Lakeside within 10 business days, with a copy to Regional Sales for in-person follow-up;
(b) Continuing to log all accountability responses in TrackWise under the existing recall record;
(c) Deferring a Round 3 effectiveness check determination until the outcome of item (a) is known, currently targeted for review by October 15, 2022.

Please let me know if either of you has questions or wants this escalated to Regulatory for direct account contact.

Priya

Sales Training Call — Speaker Notes

Date: September 27, 2021
Prepared by: Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip
Subject: Answering the Metal Ion Question — Training Notes

These notes support the September 30 field call. Please use the approved language as written where possible. The objective is to be responsive and credible without making clinical interpretations in the field.

Slide 1 — Opening

“Surgeons are seeing more questions around cobalt and chromium testing generally, including from patients who have read about metal-on-metal hips. Our role is to acknowledge the question, explain the information available in the product labeling, and connect the physician with the appropriate Veridian clinical resource when interpretation is needed.”

Do not characterize a patient’s result as normal, abnormal, concerning, or unrelated to the implant. Do not compare one patient’s value to another patient’s value.

Slide 2 — If asked: “Do ApexHip patients have elevated ions?”

Suggested response:

“Cobalt and chromium ion monitoring is an established topic across metal-on-metal hip systems and should be considered by the treating physician in the context of the individual patient. ApexHip labeling addresses follow-up and clinical evaluation considerations. We are in the process of implementing an updated label to provide additional clarity for surgeons.”

Avoid: “Apex does not cause elevated ions,” “the levels are harmless,” or “this is expected.”

If a surgeon asks whether ApexHip is the cause of a particular lab result, say:

“I can’t interpret an individual laboratory value or determine causation. I can connect you with Medical Affairs so the appropriate clinical discussion can occur.”

Route all lab-value, imaging, revision, pseudotumor, tissue-reaction, or causation questions to Medical Affairs. Do not collect or summarize clinical details by text message. Follow the complaint intake procedure if the surgeon is reporting a potential product complaint.

Slide 3 — Registry question / March 2021 NJR data

The March 2021 NJR annual report includes a five-year ApexHip revision rate of 7.1%, compared with a 3.2% class average. Do not dispute the figure, speculate about registry methodology, or provide your own explanation for the difference.

Approved framing:

“The published registry figures should be viewed in the context of broader industry variance, including patient selection, surgeon practice, follow-up patterns, and differences in reporting populations. Regulatory has reviewed the language we are using, and the updated labeling will provide additional information for clinicians.”

If pressed, repeat the published figures accurately and offer to arrange a discussion with Medical Affairs or Post-Market Surveillance. Do not say that the rate is “within normal range” or that it is “not statistically meaningful.”

Slide 4 — Label update

“The label update is in progress. It is intended to give surgeons clearer follow-up information and does not change the need for physicians to exercise their independent clinical judgment.”

Do not provide an expected approval or release date. Do not distribute draft label language.

Slide 5 — Keeping product messaging distinct

KneeFlex may be used as a simple example of product-specific messaging: “KneeFlex is a different platform and does not involve the same metal-on-metal bearing discussion.” Do not broaden that statement into a comparative safety claim or suggest that no KneeFlex issues have ever been reported.

Close with: “Be calm, be factual, and escalate clinical interpretation. We earn trust by not overreaching.”

To: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.
4400 Silver Lake Blvd
Warsaw, Indiana 46580

Subject: ISO 14242 Wear Test Report – ApexHip Supplemental Inclination Study

Dear Mr. Halvorsen:

At Veridian Orthopedics’ request, Meridian Testing Labs conducted a supplemental simulator wear study of the ApexHip metal-on-metal total hip bearing under elevated acetabular cup inclination. This work was requested as an extension of the previously completed ISO 14242 protocol testing conducted at the standard 45-degree cup orientation.

Study Objective
The objective was to compare volumetric wear, visual bearing surface condition, and cobalt/chromium release rates for ApexHip constructs tested at 55 degrees inclination against the established 45-degree control configuration.

Test Articles
Six ApexHip bearing constructs were evaluated. Test articles consisted of Co/Cr acetabular cups from the V-2100 series and matching Co/Cr femoral heads from the H-3050 series. The cup lots included V-2108, V-2113, and V-2121; head lots included H-3052, H-3057, and H-3061. Components were supplied by Veridian and inspected upon receipt for packaging integrity and visible defects. No pre-test anomalies were observed.

Methodology
Testing was performed using six-station hip joint simulators in accordance with ISO 14242 loading and motion profiles, except for the specified acetabular orientation. Three stations were configured at 45 degrees inclination and served as controls. Three stations were configured at 55 degrees inclination. All stations were operated for 5 million cycles at 1 Hz under bovine serum lubricant diluted to 25 g/L total protein concentration. Lubricant was changed at 0.5 million-cycle intervals.

Gravimetric measurements were taken at each lubricant interval after cleaning and drying pursuant to laboratory procedure MTL-WEAR-014. Lubricant samples were retained at each interval and analyzed by inductively coupled plasma mass spectrometry for cobalt and chromium content. Bearing surfaces were examined by optical microscopy at completion.

Results
The 45-degree control group demonstrated cumulative volumetric wear consistent with prior ApexHip simulator work. The 55-degree group showed a material increase beginning between 1.0 and 1.5 million cycles, with the differential increasing through the end of the study.

| Configuration | Mean Cumulative Wear at 5M Cycles | Mean Co/Cr Release Rate |
|---|---:|---:|
| 45-degree inclination | 14.2 mm³ | 0.18 mg/million cycles |
| 55-degree inclination | 71.6 mm³ | 0.94 mg/million cycles |

The elevated-inclination group therefore exhibited approximately five times the volumetric wear and metal ion release rate observed in the 45-degree control group. Two of three 55-degree stations also demonstrated localized polishing and stripe wear near the superior rim of the cup, consistent with edge-loading contact. These features were not observed to the same extent in the control group.

Conclusion
Under the conditions tested, elevated cup inclination materially increased wear of the ApexHip metal-on-metal bearing. Clinical cup positioning above approximately 50 degrees inclination presents an elevated risk of edge loading, increased wear volume, and increased cobalt/chromium release relative to the standard 45-degree orientation.

This report is provided to Mr. Halvorsen for internal distribution to the Veridian design team. It should be considered together with the applicable design inputs, risk analysis, and clinical evaluation materials.

Sincerely,

Meridian Testing Labs

Director, Biomechanical Evaluation Services

MEMORANDUM

TO: Priya Raman, Director, Quality & Complaint Handling
FROM: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
DATE: April 10, 2017
SUBJECT: Post-Launch Design Monitoring Plan – ApexHip System (DHF-0042 Appendix G)

Priya,

With the commercial US launch scheduled for next week following the Dallas sales kickoff, R&D is establishing our engineering monitoring handoff to Quality and Post-Market Surveillance. Per our discussion after the final Design Review (DR-3) sign-off, below is the proposed framework for post-market design monitoring for the ApexHip system over the initial 12 to 36 months of commercial distribution.

1. Routine Production & Lot Traceability Tracking
The transition of manufacturing from pilot runs to standard production requires routine verification of critical dimensional controls and surface specifications.
- Substrate Machining: Coordinate Measuring Machine (CMM) verification of femoral head sphericity and acetabular cup inner diameter runout will be tracked per lot on both Warsaw lines.
- Coating Lot Traceability: Incoming porous titanium material certifications for the KinetiCoat process (acquired via KBT) must maintain strict lot traceability linking raw powder lots to chamber run cycles. Static shear and tensile adhesion testing coupons (ASTM F1147 / ASTM F1044) will continue to be executed per master validation plan MVP-088. Any adhesion test yielding below nominal KBT transfer baselines will trigger an immediate quarantine of the associated cup lot (`V-2xxx` series) prior to packaging.

2. Biomechanical Wear Performance & Boundary Condition Review
As post-market clinical usage data accumulates through complaint handling and national joint registries, R&D recommends establishing a recurring schedule to cross-reference reported clinical variables against our initial design verification inputs.

Specifically, bench testing executed at Meridian Testing Labs followed the standard ISO 14242 protocol, utilizing a nominal 45° cup inclination angle under idealized anatomical alignment. However, published literature and orthopedic surgical feedback indicate that real-world acetabular component placement routinely varies, with surgeon inclination angles occasionally exceeding 50° to 55° depending on patient anatomy and surgical approach.

Given the metal-on-metal (Co/Cr on Co/Cr) articulation and the hydrodynamic lubrication regime of large-diameter heads (36–50 mm), steep inclination can disrupt fluid-film lubrication and induce localized rim contact or edge-loading. I recommend that R&D and Quality schedule a formal re-evaluation of wear performance data within 18 to 24 months post-launch. If early post-market registries or explant retrievals show unexplained wear patterns, we should consider commissioning supplementary simulator testing at elevated inclination angles (e.g., 50° and 55°) to establish empirical wear-rate boundaries outside standard ISO 14242 parameters.

3. Complaint Volume Thresholds and Escalation Triggers
To ensure seamless integration with TrackWise, the following design-related escalation triggers are proposed for incoming field reports:
- Mechanical Complaints: Any report of taper fretting, stem loosening, or cup displacement exceeding an incidence rate of 0.25% of distributed units within the first 12 months will be escalated directly to the ApexHip design team.
- Biocompatibility / Tissue Response: Any report citing unexplained local soft tissue inflammation, effusion, or early revision without mechanical loosening should be flagged under code COMP-BIO for joint review by Quality and Clinical Affairs.
- Instrument Fit: Intraoperative reports concerning apex impactor seating or cup holder release will be reviewed monthly to determine if tooling tolerances require an ECO.

Please let me know if this framework aligns with your team's post-market procedures so we can finalize the sign-offs in Agile ahead of next Monday.

Regards,

Tom Halvorsen
Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.

INTERNAL MEMORANDUM

Date: February 5, 2024
From: Owen Park, Chief Financial Officer
To: File / Finance Leadership Distribution
Subject: Reserve Adequacy Reassessment — Apex Product Liability

1. Purpose

This memo documents my recommendation to increase the ApexHip product liability reserve from its current balance of $18.0M (booked Q3 2022) to $45.0M, effective immediately, in light of developments following the February 2, 2024 voluntary market withdrawal announcement.

2. Background

The original $18M reserve was established in Q3 2022 based on early claims volume and an actuarial model that assumed a relatively contained litigation footprint. Since MDL 3102 (N.D. Ind.) was formed in December 2023, the docket has grown quickly. As of this week we have 340 plaintiffs on file, and our outside actuary (working with Whitfield & Barr on case characteristics) projects continued growth given the withdrawal announcement, which plaintiffs' counsel are already characterizing publicly as an admission.

3. Updated Actuarial Input

Rachel's team and W&B provided updated per-case settlement range estimates of $75,000–$250,000, reflecting revision surgery costs, ARMD-related damages, and comparable MoM hip litigation outcomes elsewhere in the industry. Applying a blended weighted average across the current plaintiff population, plus a projected filing curve through year-end, produces an estimated ultimate exposure materially above our current reserve. Legal defense cost projections (W&B lead counsel plus local counsel in coordinated proceedings) add a further meaningful component — MDLs of this size do not resolve cheaply or quickly.

4. Insurance Position

Aegis Specialty issued its notice of circumstance and reservation of rights following our 2022 notification. Aegis has not denied coverage but has reserved on several bases, including product-line exclusions under review and allocation questions given the multi-year exposure period. We carry a $10M self-insured retention before any Aegis coverage attaches, meaning the company bears the first $10M of losses directly regardless of how the coverage dispute resolves. I am not building in any assumed insurance offset in this reserve calculation until Aegis's position is clarified in writing.

5. Recommendation

I recommend increasing the reserve to $45.0M, reflecting:
- Current plaintiff count (340) and expected near-term growth,
- Settlement range midpoint applied across expected case mix,
- Estimated defense costs through anticipated bellwether proceedings,
- No insurance offset pending Aegis's coverage determination.

This increase will be reflected as a charge in Q1 2024 results and disclosed in the Q1 2024 Form 10-Q, including appropriate contingency language coordinated with Rachel's office regarding the MDL, the withdrawal, and reserve methodology.

6. Ongoing Monitoring

Given the pace of filings, I recommend we move to a quarterly reassessment cadence rather than our prior annual review, at minimum through the resolution of initial bellwether cases. I'll ask Hannah to build a standing tracker tying plaintiff count, filing velocity, and settlement data to reserve adequacy each quarter so we're not caught flat-footed again.

Happy to walk through the model assumptions with anyone who wants detail before we finalize the Q1 numbers.

Owen

Date: January 10, 2019
From: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
To: Priya Raman, Director, Quality & Complaint Handling
Cc: Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip
Subject: Proposal to re-run ApexHip wear testing at higher inclination angles

Priya, Carlos —

I want to formally propose a new round of wear testing on ApexHip at 55-degree cup inclination, and I'd like to get this scoped with Meridian Testing Labs sooner rather than later.

Some background for the file, though you both know most of this. Back at DR-3 in November 2016 we approved the wear-test protocol per ISO 14242 at the standard 45-degree inclination only. At the time that was defensible — it matched the predicate testing approach and the schedule didn't have room for a broader matrix. But in my 2017 post-launch monitoring memo I flagged that we should revisit inclination sensitivity about two years out, once we had real surgical placement data instead of bench assumptions. We're basically at that mark now.

Since launch I've been keeping an informal tracker of retrieval and imaging data where I can get it — mostly from explants and a few surgeon-shared fluoroscopy measurements, not a formal study, so treat it as directional. What it's showing is a meaningful cluster of cups implanted well outside the 45-degree target, some pushing 55 degrees or more, which is not surprising given how much placement varies case to case in the field. That's exactly the scenario our current test matrix doesn't cover.

I also can't ignore the Atlanta cluster Priya's team logged last August — three patients out of Dr. Feld's practice with elevated metal-ion complaints. I'm not saying inclination angle explains all three, and I know complaint handling is looking at this from the clinical side, but from a design standpoint it lines up with what edge-loading literature predicts: higher wear rates at higher inclination due to rim contact. If our bench testing has only ever validated the low end of the placement range surgeons are actually using, that's a gap we should close before it becomes a bigger problem.

Concretely, I'm asking for:

1. Budget approval for a supplemental wear-test run at 55-degree inclination, ISO 14242-based methodology, using the same head/cup combinations tested originally so we have a clean comparison.
2. Lab time with Meridian — I've had an informal conversation with their test engineer and they think they could slot us in by early Q2 if we commit soon.
3. Priya's team's input on what complaint/retrieval data would be useful to fold into the test rationale for the file.
4. Carlos, mainly a heads-up at this stage — I don't think this needs to touch messaging yet, but I wanted you looped in given any downstream implications for positioning if results come back different from the 45-degree data.

I'd estimate this is a $60–80K test program depending on sample size, plus lab turnaround of roughly 10–12 weeks. I know that's not trivial, but I'd rather we generate this data proactively than have it show up in a registry report or an FDA letter first.

Happy to walk through the tracker data in person if useful — I can bring the spreadsheet.

Tom

SUBJECT: Voluntary Permanent Market Withdrawal – ApexHip Total Hip System (510(k) K162447)

Dear CDRH Office of Compliance:

This letter serves as formal notification that Veridian Orthopedics, Inc. ("Veridian") has initiated a voluntary permanent market withdrawal of the ApexHip Total Hip System, originally cleared under 510(k) K162447 on March 9, 2017. Effective February 2, 2024, Veridian has ceased all commercial distribution and sales of all components of the ApexHip system across all domestic and international markets.

Veridian has structured and initiated the following actions pursuant to 21 CFR Part 806:

1. Scope and Distinction from Prior Regulatory Actions: This voluntary withdrawal encompasses all sizes and lots of the ApexHip acetabular cups (sizes 44–62 mm), femoral heads (sizes 36–50 mm), and associated femoral stems. Please note that this comprehensive commercial withdrawal is separate and distinct from the prior voluntary Class II recall initiated on June 14, 2022 (Recall Number Z-1418-2022), which was strictly confined to cup lots V-2200 through V-2299 concerning KinetiCoat plasma-spray adhesion anomalies.

2. Underlying Basis for Withdrawal: Ongoing evaluation of cumulative post-market surveillance data, specifically longitudinal data sets published in external joint registries including the UK National Joint Registry (NJR) and the American Joint Replacement Registry (AJRR), indicates an elevated long-term cumulative revision rate associated with metal-on-metal articulation that exceeds acceptable comparative class performance thresholds. While previous labeling updates and clinical communications sought to address surgical technique and patient selection parameters, Veridian has determined that permanent cessation of sales is the appropriate risk-mitigation measure.

3. Field Correction and Inventory Quarantine: All regional sales offices, contract distributors, and hospital consignments have been formally instructed to cease implantation immediately. Field representatives have initiated the physical recovery and return of all non-implanted inventory to our central distribution facility in Warsaw, Indiana, where products will be placed under strict QA quarantine pending destruction.

4. Surgeon and Facility Notification: Direct written communication to all operating surgeons, risk management departments, and hospital purchasing administrators is underway, providing monitoring guidance and clinical follow-up recommendations for existing implanted patients.

Veridian will provide the CDRH Office of Compliance with bi-weekly progress reports detailing inventory reconciliation and customer notification confirmation until final closeout.

Respectfully submitted,

Dana Okonkwo
Vice President, Regulatory Affairs
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.

21 CFR Part 803

Report Date: 14 December 2021
Prepared By: Devon Mitchell, Sr. Regulatory Specialist
Product: ApexHip Metal-on-Metal Total Hip System
Patient Identifier: JW-1102
Facility: Denver Orthopedic Center, Denver, Colorado
Reporter: James Whitaker, M.D.
Initial Manufacturer Report: Yes
Event Type: Serious Injury / Device Revision

1. EVENT DATE AND AWARENESS

Date of event: 02 December 2021
Date Veridian became aware: 06 December 2021
TrackWise Complaint No.: TW-2021-1189
MDR Reportability Determination: Reportable under 21 CFR 803.50(a)(1).

2. DEVICE INFORMATION

Implant date: 18 May 2018
Revision date: 02 December 2021
Implanted components reported:

| Component | Catalog Description | Lot No. |
|---|---|---|
| Femoral head | ApexHip Co/Cr femoral head | H-3105 |
| Acetabular cup | ApexHip KinetiCoat-coated Co/Cr cup | V-2087 |

The explanted head and cup were retained by Denver Orthopedic Center for return to Veridian. The cup lot is not within the V-2200 through V-2299 manufacturing population subsequently identified for coating review. No allegation of coating flaking or loss of fixation was provided by the reporting surgeon.

3. EVENT NARRATIVE

Dr. Whitaker reported that patient JW-1102 presented with progressive groin pain, swelling, and reduced range of motion approximately three years after primary implantation. Pre-revision laboratory testing reportedly showed elevated cobalt levels; the surgeon reported serum cobalt of 12.4 µg/L. Chromium was also described as elevated, although a final value was not provided at the time of this report.

At revision, Dr. Whitaker observed a substantial periarticular soft-tissue mass characterized as consistent with pseudotumor, with dark fluid and areas of tissue discoloration. The surgeon reported debridement of affected tissue and removal of the ApexHip acetabular cup and femoral head. The femoral stem was retained. No infection was reported. Pathology results, if available, have been requested.

Based on information presently available, metal-on-metal bearing wear and associated metal debris are suspected contributors to the elevated metal-ion findings and local tissue reaction. The specific mechanism of wear has not been confirmed pending evaluation of returned components and receipt of operative, laboratory, and pathology records.

4. FOLLOW-UP ACTIONS

Veridian has requested return of the explanted components, operative report, cobalt/chromium laboratory results, and pathology findings. Complaint investigation remains open in TrackWise. A supplemental MDR will be submitted if additional information changes the reportability assessment or provides relevant device evaluation findings.

Devon Mitchell
Sr. Regulatory Specialist
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.

Re: Marketing claim history summary for MDL response

Elena:

Per our discussion, below is the requested high-level chronology of ApexHip marketing claims and the supporting review materials. This is intended to assist W&B in preparing the company’s response concerning historical promotional messaging.

1. Launch materials (2017–2018). At U.S. launch in April 2017, the principal positioning was directed to active adults ages 45–65 and emphasized large-head stability, low wear, and intended longevity. The original “Active Life” materials used variations of “built for an active life” and “designed for lasting movement.” Claim substantiation files maintained by Marketing Communications include the 510(k) clearance materials, ISO wear-testing summaries, and clinical literature then cited by the team.

2. “Lifetime of movement” language (2019–2021). The phrase “designed to last a lifetime of movement” first appears in the Kessler Reid brochure draft circulated in August 2019 and was carried into the 2020 Active Life campaign, certain booth graphics, and digital copy. Anika Shah’s claim substantiation review reflects that Regulatory requested qualification of the statement as an aspirational durability claim rather than a guarantee. The final consumer-facing materials included qualifying language, although use was not perfectly uniform across field collateral.

3. Revision-rate comparisons (2020–2021). Comparative revision-rate language was introduced in sales and surgeon-facing slide materials during 2020. Those materials generally described ApexHip’s early performance and, in some versions, compared revision experience with published class or registry data. The underlying review file includes a March 2020 substantiation memorandum, source citations, and drafts reflecting comments from Regulatory, Clinical, and Marketing. Following the March 2021 NJR report, the comparison language was reviewed again. By fall 2021, materials using favorable comparative revision messaging were retired or revised.

4. Retirement and withdrawal. The “lifetime of movement” tagline was removed from newly produced materials during the 2021 label-update and messaging review. Existing field pieces were subject to retrieval and replacement instructions thereafter. Following the February 2, 2024 voluntary market withdrawal, Marketing discontinued ApexHip promotional activity entirely.

The relevant materials should include the Kessler Reid creative files, Shah’s substantiation review memoranda, version-controlled brochures and web copy, and the 2020–2021 sales decks. TO: Dana Okonkwo (VP, Regulatory Affairs), Rachel Steinberg (General Counsel), Dr. Leon Adeyemi (Chief Medical Officer), Marcus Lee (VP, Sales)
FROM: Carlos Mendes (Product Manager, ApexHip)
DATE: September 28, 2021
SUBJECT: Draft "Dear Doctor" Letter – ApexHip Acetabular System Labeling Update

Following the decisions reached during our September 14 Registry Signal Review meeting, I have prepared the initial draft text for the upcoming customer notification ("Dear Doctor" letter) regarding the ApexHip Total Hip System.

As agreed by the review team and executive leadership, Veridian will maintain active commercial distribution of ApexHip while implementing an immediate Instructions for Use (IFU) labeling update to address emerging registry trends.

Background & Signal Summary
The primary driver for this communication is data presented from the March 2021 National Joint Registry (NJR) 17th Annual Report, which identified a cumulative 5-year revision rate of 7.1% for the ApexHip construct, compared to an average class benchmark of approximately 3.2% across contemporary metal-on-metal (MoM) hip resurfacing and total replacement systems. While internal clinical evaluations indicate that well-positioned constructs continue to demonstrate strong clinical survivorship, registry data and internal engineering assessments correlate early revisions predominantly with adverse local tissue reactions (ALTR/ARMD) linked to elevated cobalt and chromium ion levels.

Proposed Letter Content & Labeling Guidance
The draft notification emphasizes patient safety, precise surgical technique, and targeted post-operative vigilance:

1. Patient Monitoring Recommendations: We advise clinicians to establish heightened routine clinical and radiographic follow-up protocols for all implanted ApexHip patients, with particular attention to individuals receiving larger femoral head diameters (≥44 mm). Routine cross-sectional imaging (MARS-MRI or ultrasound) and periodic blood metal-ion quantification (whole blood cobalt and chromium) should be considered annually or upon any presentation of unexplained pain, clicking, or swelling.
2. Surgical Positioning & Angle Inclination: Revisions strongly correlate with edge-loading phenomena. The revised labeling explicitly instructs surgeons to target an acetabular cup inclination angle within 40° to 45° and anteversion between 15° and 20°. Operating outside these ranges—specifically exceeding 50° of operative abduction—markedly increases the risk of accelerated fluid-film wear and premature component loosening.

Next Steps & Timeline
Our target mail date to all US and EU implanting orthopedic surgeons, chief medical officers, and relevant risk management personnel is mid-October 2021. Reps will receive accompanying talking points once this text is locked.

Please review the attached formal notification layout (`Apex_Dear_Doctor_Draft_v1.docx`) and provide your redlines. We require formal sign-off from Regulatory Affairs, Legal, and Clinical before Dana submits the final package to the agency and we proceed with mass distribution.

Re: Notification of Labeling Update – ApexHip Total Hip System
510(k) K162447

To Whom It May Concern:

Veridian Orthopedics, Inc. is providing notice of a voluntary labeling update for the ApexHip Total Hip System, cleared under 510(k) K162447 on March 9, 2017.

Following Veridian’s September 14, 2021 Registry Signal Review, the Company elected to clarify the Instructions for Use and surgeon-facing labeling regarding patient follow-up and monitoring where postoperative cup inclination angles are high. This action follows review of post-market registry information, including the March 2021 annual report of the United Kingdom National Joint Registry (NJR), which reported a five-year revision rate of 7.1% for ApexHip compared with a 3.2% class average.

The revised labeling will include the following clarification:

1. Surgeons should consider postoperative radiographic assessment of acetabular component position, including inclination angle, as part of routine clinical follow-up.

2. For patients with high cup inclination angles, physicians should consider closer clinical follow-up and evaluation for symptoms potentially associated with elevated metal ion exposure or adverse local tissue reaction.

3. Where clinically indicated, evaluation may include serum cobalt and chromium testing, cross-sectional imaging, and/or referral for additional assessment consistent with the treating physician’s clinical judgment.

The update does not alter the device’s indications for use, contraindications, materials, manufacturing process, sterilization method, intended use, or design specifications. No physical change has been made to the ApexHip Total Hip System. The revision is intended to provide additional clarification to surgeons based on post-market information and does not represent a design change.

Veridian has assessed the labeling revision under 21 CFR 807.81(a)(3) and FDA’s guidance regarding when to submit a new 510(k) for a change to an existing device. Veridian concludes that a new premarket notification is not required because the change is limited to labeling clarification and does not affect safety or effectiveness in a manner that could significantly affect the device’s safety or effectiveness, nor does it constitute a major change or modification in intended use.

We intend to distribute the revised Instructions for Use and an accompanying Dear Doctor communication to ApexHip customers during October 2021. The revised labeling and supporting assessment have been retained in the ApexHip design history file.

Please contact me if the Office of Compliance has questions or requires additional information.

Sincerely,

PRESENTATION NOTES
Veridian Orthopedics — Reconstructive Sales Training
Objection Handling Module, Q2 2021

Prepared by: Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip
Date: April 14, 2021
Audience: Regional sales managers and field reps (Reconstructive), for regional rollout April–May 2021
Accompanying deck: Objection_Handling_Q2_2021_v3.pptx

Purpose of this module

Following the March 2021 NJR annual report, we're anticipating more surgeons and hospital purchasing contacts will ask about ApexHip's five-year revision rate (reported at 7.1% vs. a 3.2% class average). This module gives reps a consistent, compliant way to respond. Please review with your team before any customer-facing conversations reference registry data.

Slide 4 — Acknowledging the NJR figure

Do not deny or minimize the registry number if a surgeon raises it directly — they may already have the report in hand. Instead, acknowledge and contextualize:

- "We're aware of the NJR data and we take registry signals seriously. Registries are a valuable but imperfect tool — cohort size, surgical technique variation, and patient selection all factor into revision rates across any implant system."
- Suggested phrasing: "Every device has a learning curve, and patient selection matters — outcomes with ApexHip, like any hip system, are strongly influenced by inclination angle and case selection at implantation."
- Redirect to Veridian's ongoing PMS activity: "Our team continuously monitors real-world performance and we're committed to sharing updates as they develop."

Slide 5 — Hard boundaries (read carefully)

Reps must NOT:
- Promise or imply outcomes ("this won't happen to your patients," "you won't see this issue")
- Discuss, confirm, or deny the existence of any ongoing complaint investigation, MDR filing, or internal review
- Speculate about root cause of the registry finding
- Provide comparative revision-rate statistics not pre-approved by Regulatory/Marketing

If a surgeon or purchasing contact pushes for specifics beyond the approved talking points, the answer is: "That's a great question for our medical affairs team — let me get you connected." Do not freelance an answer. Flag the interaction to your regional manager and to me afterward so we can track frequency and content of these conversations.

Slide 6 — Purchasing/GPO conversations

Similar posture. Purchasing contacts (e.g., VantageOne-affiliated accounts) may cite registry data during contract renewal discussions. Reps should stick to the same acknowledge-and-redirect framework — do not get pulled into pricing concessions justified by clinical performance claims.

Slide 9 — KneeFlex competitive positioning (unrelated segment)

Separate topic, included in this module for scheduling efficiency since most regional trainings cover both products back-to-back. Key messaging pillars for KneeFlex against the Zimmer and Stryker competitive set: instrumentation simplicity, faster OR time, and the updated tibial tray geometry from the 2020 running change. No registry or objection-handling issues currently associated with KneeFlex — this slide is purely competitive positioning, not defensive.

Next steps

Regional managers to schedule team sessions by April 30. Please route any surgeon questions you can't answer with the approved language to me or to Dr. Adeyemi's office rather than improvising. I'll circulate an FAQ addendum once we have more of these conversations logged.

— Carlos

Design History File — Engineering Memorandum

To: Priya Raman, Director, Quality & Complaint Handling; Carlos Mendes, Product Manager, ApexHip
From: Tom Halvorsen, Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip
Date: September 3, 2019
Subject: ApexHip Wear Test Re-Analysis — 55° Cup Inclination Re-Run — DHF Reference
DHF Item: ApexHip Wear Testing / ECO-2019-118 (proposed)

1. Purpose

This memo documents the results of the February 2019 wear-test re-run performed at Meridian Testing Labs on the ApexHip cup/head/liner assembly at a 55° cup inclination angle, and evaluates whether the original DR-3 wear-test protocol (ISO 14242, standard 45° inclination only, approved November 2016) adequately characterizes in-vivo wear behavior across the clinically observed range of implanted cup positions.

2. Background

The original wear-test protocol tested only at the nominal 45° inclination angle specified in ISO 14242. This was consistent with predicate practice at the time and was accepted at DR-3. However, published literature and internal complaint review (including the Atlanta cluster logged in TrackWise beginning August 2018) raised the question of whether cups implanted at higher inclination angles — which do occur clinically, particularly with less experienced surgical technique or difficult anatomy — see meaningfully higher wear rates due to edge-loading of the femoral head against the cup rim.

3. Test Summary

I re-ran the standard ISO 14242 wear protocol at 55° cup inclination (10° above nominal) using the same lot of test articles as our original 45° baseline (36mm and 40mm head diameters, KinetiCoat-coated cups). Results are attached as Apex_wear_55deg_rev2.xlsx.

Key finding: volumetric wear rate at 55° inclination was 4 to 6 times higher than at the standard 45° condition, depending on head diameter (higher multiplier at smaller head sizes). This is consistent with edge-loading mechanics — at higher inclination, contact stress concentrates at the cup rim rather than distributing across the bearing surface, which for a metal-on-metal couple can accelerate both wear and Co/Cr ion release.

4. Discussion

I want to be careful not to overstate what a bench test tells us about clinical risk, but the magnitude here is large enough that I think we need to treat it seriously. A 4-6x wear multiplier at 55° suggests that patients whose cups end up positioned in that range — for whatever reason, surgical technique, anatomy, or drift over time — could be experiencing substantially elevated metal debris exposure compared to what our 45°-only testing predicted.

I don't think this is necessarily a acute safety issue for every implanted patient, since we don't yet know what fraction of the implanted population actually sits above 50-55° inclination. But it does mean our design verification testing understated real-world wear risk for a meaningful subset of cases.

5. Proposed Design Change Evaluation — ECO-2019-118

I am proposing that we open ECO-2019-118 to evaluate design changes intended to reduce edge-loading sensitivity at high inclination, including:

- Increasing head diameter recommendations (larger heads generally show more favorable arc-of-coverage relative to rim contact)
- Modifying cup rim geometry / coverage angle
- Revisiting labeling/instructions for use regarding acceptable cup positioning tolerance

6. Recommendation

Before committing engineering resources to a design change, I recommend a clinical correlation study — ideally using registry data or explant analysis where available — to determine whether elevated inclination angles are actually associated with the complaint pattern we're seeing, and at what frequency high-inclination placements occur in the field. Without that correlation, we risk chasing a bench-test artifact rather than a real clinical driver.

I've copied Priya and Carlos so this is captured in the DHF and available for complaint trending cross-reference. I'd like to discuss timing and resourcing for the correlation study at the next design review.

Tom Halvorsen
Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip

Re: Recall Closure Request — Z-1418-2022, ApexHip Acetabular Cup Lots V-2200–V-2299

To Whom It May Concern:

Veridian Orthopedics, Inc. respectfully requests termination of recall status for the voluntary Class II recall initiated June 14, 2022, identified by FDA Recall Number Z-1418-2022.

The recall applied to ApexHip acetabular cups, lots V-2200 through V-2299, manufactured at our Cork, Ireland facility and distributed in the United States. A total of 1,140 units were distributed. As of October 14, 2022, all but a small number of units have been retrieved or otherwise accounted for through customer inventory reconciliation and documented disposition. The remaining units are with accounts that have provided written confirmation that the affected product is no longer available for use and has been quarantined pending final return processing.

Recall notifications were issued to all direct accounts, distributors, and consignees. Veridian conducted follow-up communications and effectiveness checks in accordance with 21 CFR Part 7. The final effectiveness-check response rate was 98.6%; nonresponding accounts were subject to repeated outreach and inventory verification through their purchasing or materials-management departments.

The underlying issue was identified as plasma-spray parameter drift following chamber maintenance. Corrective and preventive action CAPA-2022-0091 addressed chamber requalification requirements, parameter controls, operator verification, and enhanced incoming inspection. CAPA effectiveness checks have been completed and passed. Review of post-implementation production and inspection records did not identify recurrence of coating adhesion failures.

Two MDR reports related to Denver operating-room cases involving affected product were submitted to FDA under 21 CFR Part 803. Both reports have been acknowledged by FDA.

Based on completion of notification, product recovery and accountability activities, and verified corrective action effectiveness, Veridian requests that FDA terminate the recall status for Z-1418-2022. Supporting records are available upon request.

Sincerely,

Dana Okonkwo
Vice President, Regulatory Affairs
Veridian Orthopedics, Inc.

ECO-2019-118 — ApexHip Acetabular Cup Design Change (Deferred)
Meeting Date: December 14, 2020
Location: Warsaw, IN — Engineering Conference Room B / Teams
Minutes prepared by: Tom Halvorsen

Attendees: Tom Halvorsen (Sr. Design Engineer, ApexHip), Priya Raman (Director, Quality & Complaint Handling), Carlos Mendes (Product Manager, ApexHip), Dana Okonkwo (VP Regulatory Affairs)

1. Purpose
Re-review of ECO-2019-118 (proposed cup/liner geometry change to address edge-loading wear identified in 2019 55° inclination testing), originally deferred at DR review in 2019. Meeting called to reassess in light of updated complaint trend data.

2. Discussion

2.1 Complaint trend data. Raman presented updated TrackWise trending showing a continued gradual increase in metal-ion-related complaints since the 2018 Atlanta cluster, with additional isolated reports logged from Denver and Nashville territories through Q3 2020. Raman noted the trend remains within historical variability per current procedure but acknowledged the slope has not flattened.

2.2 Wear test results. Halvorsen reviewed the 2019 55° inclination re-test data (originally reported in the Feb 2019 memo to Raman/Mendes) showing 4–6x wear at higher cup inclination angles versus the standard 45° protocol used for 510(k) clearance. No new bench testing has been performed since; data referenced is unchanged from 2019.

2.3 Cost of implementation. Halvorsen presented updated cost estimate for implementing the proposed liner geometry change. Original 2019 estimate was approximately $260,000. Due to tooling changes at the Cork facility since that time (new fixturing installed for an unrelated coating process change), current estimate has risen to approximately $410,000, driven by re-tooling and requalification of injection/machining tooling.

2.4 Registry data. Okonkwo noted the NJR annual report covering ApexHip's 5-year outcomes is expected in early 2021 and will provide updated revision-rate data relevant to this decision. Mendes agreed that this data would materially inform messaging and design prioritization.

3. Resolutions

3.1 The design change under ECO-2019-118 is again deferred. The team concluded that implementing the change at this time is not warranted given (a) complaint trend data remains within procedural thresholds, (b) increased cost of implementation ($410,000), and (c) the imminent availability of NJR registry data expected Q1 2021, which should inform the scope and urgency of any design action.

3.2 The team will reconvene promptly following receipt of the NJR report to reassess ECO-2019-118 in light of the new data.

4. Action Items
- Okonkwo to circulate NJR report upon receipt (Owner: Okonkwo)
- Raman to continue monthly trend monitoring (Owner: Raman)
- Halvorsen to hold current cost estimate on file (Owner: Halvorsen)

Next review: upon receipt of NJR data, tentatively Q1 2021.

Reporting Period: January 1–March 31, 2022
Subject: Q1 2022 metal-ion complaint trending summary

Per the complaint-trending procedure, Quality reviewed all ApexHip complaints closed or opened during Q1 2022 with reported elevated cobalt and/or chromium values, suspected ARMD, tissue reaction, or revision associated with metal debris. Duplicate reports concerning the same patient event were consolidated where identifiable.

A total of 19 metal-ion-related ApexHip complaints were recorded during Q1 2022, compared with 12 during Q1 2021. The increase is concentrated in territories where the product has historically had greater utilization and where follow-up laboratory values are being obtained more consistently.

| Region | Q1 2022 Complaints | Revision Outcome Reported |
|---|---:|---:|
| Southeast | 7 | 5 |
| Nashville | 4 | 3 |
| Denver | 3 | 2 |
| Other | 5 | 4 |
| Total | 19 | 14 |

Of the 19 complaints, 14 include confirmation that revision surgery occurred or had been scheduled based on the latest information provided by the treating facility or surgeon. The remaining five reports involve ongoing surveillance, imaging, repeat laboratory testing, or a recommendation for clinical follow-up. Complaint files remain subject to update as additional operative and explant information is received.

Serum cobalt values were available in 16 of the 19 complaint records. The average reported serum cobalt level among those complainants was 41 ppb. This is materially above the generally cited normal range of less than 1 ppb in individuals without a cobalt-containing implant. Chromium values were also elevated in a majority of records, although reporting units and collection timing were not uniform enough to calculate a comparable aggregate without further normalization.

The observed trend continues to track with the pattern Halvorsen’s engineering team identified in prior wear testing, including increased wear under non-standard cup positioning conditions. Quality is continuing to process each event per procedure, including MDR assessment where applicable, and will provide the underlying TrackWise extract to Regulatory and PMS for their respective review.

Under 21 CFR 803.50(a), a report is required if we become aware of information reasonably suggesting the device (1) may have caused or contributed to a death or serious injury, or (2) has malfunctioned and would be likely to cause or contribute to a death or serious injury if the malfunction recurred. Elevated serum cobalt alone, without a confirmed malfunction (e.g., coating failure, wear debris finding) or a confirmed serious injury (e.g., biopsy-confirmed ARMD, revision), does not on its face meet either prong. Lab values trending high can reflect normal wear within expected ranges.

That said, three complaints from one practice in a short window is the kind of pattern that deserves a written analysis, not just a verbal judgment call.
